The original allocation of $400,000 for the fiscal year 1950-51 was voted on June 30, 1950, in the further supplementary estimates of that year to provide for Canadian participation in the technical assistance program to June 30, 1951.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (SI. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house adjourned on Tuesday evening I was reviewing some remarks that had been made in this debate on external affairs by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and was drawing the attention of the house especially to the latter part of the hon. member's remarks to be found on page 690 of Hansard. I now wish to refer to that portion of his speech in which the hon. member said that he knew it was a bit risky to discuss Far Eastern questions and then went on to make reference to Owen Lattimore in the United States. During the course of that debate I stated that I had heard of Owen Lattimore long before I had heard of Senator McCarthy, and the impression I had of Owen Lattimore was that he was a fellow traveller and that his writings leaned to the left.

External Affairs
Since Tuesday evening I have found an article in the China Monthly, published in New York in October, 1948, in which there is a review of two books published by two men who had been sent to China by the United States government during the years following the conclusion of the war with Japan. These two books are "The Stilwell Papers", which contains the memoirs of General Stilwell as edited by Theodore White, and "The United States and China", by John King Fairbank. This article by Alfred Kohl-berg is illustrated, and the first picture I see is a picture of Owen Lattimore sitting down with Chiang Kai-shek in Chungking. The author of this article is also the publisher of a magazine called Plain Talk and chairman of the American China Policy Association, I quote from this article as follows:
Early in 1943, Lattimore wrote of the generalissimo . we have in Asia a world statesman, a real genius in Chiang Kai-shek. What may be called the functional test of the historical importance of Chiang Kai-shek is the fact that throughout an already long political career, he has grown steadily greater and greater." The following year, after orders from Moscow to switch, Lattimore switched his opinions to suit.
That is by Kohlberg.

This is the article by Kohlberg. Later in the article Lattimore is named as being associated with Alger Hiss, Lauchlin Currie, Edgar Snow and John Carter Vincent who had planned to slowly choke to death and destroy the government of the republic of China and build up the Chinese communists for post-war success.
I feel that Chiang Kai-shek needs no defence in this house, or indeed in America. Chiang Kai-shek was the head of one of the many nations that we considered as being united nations during world war II. His military record and speeches are there for anyone to investigate. He was a loyal ally. I think it is a disgrace for us not only to have deserted him in his hour of need but to malign him at the present time.
I am aware that in a general review such as was being given toy the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) he may be excused for making minor mistakes, but I do not think justice and truth should permit the gross mistakes that are to be found in his speech as reported on page 690. He stated, and I drew this to the attention of the house on Tuesday, that five years ago-that is in 1947-Owen Lattimore had warned' the country that Chiang Kai-shek was out and that the Chinese people would have nothing further to do with him.
The hon. gentleman knows full well that there have been volumes written on United

States-Chinese negotiations and there is certainly a very strong case to be made out that China was deserted by the United States and that United States officials who visited China interfered with the war effort of Chiang Kai-shek and brought about a result which led to the Chinese communist government taking over that country.
They provided him with arms.

I know the hon. gentleman said that they supplied him with billions of dollars' worth, but I challenge him to prove his statement by any documentary evidence. I have here an article that appeared in February, 1948, in Fortune called "The Tyrannous Decade." This goes at great length into relations between the United States and China. If the hon. member will read that and the other voluminous documents available I think he will find that, in the fight against Japan, China was a valuable ally. China was a valuable ally from the time Japan turned on the United States in December, 1941, until the time Russia entered the war one week before the war with Japan concluded.
Then from V-J day 1945, until September 1948, there was not a dollar's worth of aid sent by the United States to China to help Chiang Kai-shek. Naturally we could expect that when China was fighting Japan and at the time when the United States was fighting Japan, the United States would see to it that China was assisted in a fight in which they were both engaged; but Chinese sympathizers with Chiang Kai-shek are not slow to point out that prior to the attack at Pearl Harbor the United States was sending war materials to Japan, especially in the form of scrap, which enabled that country to build up its munitions supply.
So was Canada.

So was
Canada, the hon. member says. I do not think that is anything for us to be proud of. In this same magazine there is a picture showing General Marshall, who is supposed to have said the same thing as Owen Lattimore about the Chinese nationalist government being useless, and General Marshall is standing with General Chang-Chun and General Chou En-lai of the Chinese communists. The caption on the picture is "Shotgun Marriage." General Marshall was sent out to China to force General Chiang Kai-shek into making an agreement with the communists. It was that agreement that helped to weaken General Chiang Kai-shek's military forces. The fact that Chiang Kai-shek did not get military aid in time.helped

to defeat the nationalist armies, and left us with the terrible situation we have there today.
Someone has said that it is a strange thing to see Germany, Italy and Japan, the three nations we were fighting in world war II, now riding on the crest of the wave and all soon to be our allies, while Poland, the country for whom we went to war, and China, our ally in the same world war II, are smothered by the communists. The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar I am sure has not forgotten that the Russians came into the war in the Pacific a week before it ended. They went into Manchuria, and would not allow the United States to enter.
By agreement with Chiang Kai-shek.

No, but by
agreement between Churchill and Roosevelt and Stalin at Yalta the year before. This agreement was made in February, 1945, at Yalta, and it was agreed that Russia was to get back all she had lost in the Russian-Japanese war of 1904. It was the greatest mistake ever made by any statesman, and the greatest miscalculation; because the week after the Russians entered the war, Japan capitulated. At that time military equipment owned by the Japanese armies in Manchuria, all that great storehouse of munitions, came into the possession of the Russians and was passed over by the Russians to the Chinese communists. Before the Russians entered the war there was not a Chinese communist in Manchuria; yet that great territory, the richest part of China, was immediately entered by the Chinese communists. They were armed with the equipment taken from the Japanese, and with other equipment given by the Russians, whereas, as I have already pointed out, Chiang Kai-shek, between V-J day and 1948, received no assistance whatever from the United States.
Instead of assistance, the nationalists received a great deal of embarrassment from some of the officials who were sent, including General Marshall. I do not say that when General Marshall went there he did not have good intentions. I say he was misled. We are all aware of the great controversy that has raged in the United States over the state department. It was a surprise to many people when North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950 to find that the United States reversed its policy and went to the assistance of South Korea. They are still defending them against the attack of the North Koreans, trained by the Russians, and the Chinese communists who have been sent there by their Russian masters. The hon. member mentions billions of dollars being sent by
External Affairs
the United States to Chiang Kai-shek. There is an incident told about the state department printing billions of dollars of worthless Chinese money and sending that into China. I do not know if my hon. friend was referring to those worthless billions when he was talking about the billions of dollars, or whether he was referring to the money sent to China before V-J day when China was an ally of the United States.
It seems to me that the hon. member has reason to revise his opinion. I find it very easy to listen to the hon. member. He is a good speaker, and a plausible speaker. I am afraid that, with some people, he is a convincing speaker. I suggest, however, that there are a great many statements in this speech which he cannot justify. He says that, unfortunately, support of the corrupt regime now in Formosa drove the Chinese literally into the arms of the Soviet union-drove the supporters of the nationalist army into the arms of the communists! We cannot say the same thing about Poland, Roumania or Hungary, all those countries that are in the arms of the Soviets today. It was our mistake in policy. We worshipped at the shrine of Stalin to such a degree that we put these people in the arms of the Russians.
There is another gentleman who went to China, General Chennault, whose famous Flying Tigers fought for Chiang Kai-shek. In an article that is quoted in the Catholic Digest for April, 1952, at page 56, he says:
The great masses of the Chinese people never sought communism. Their leaders were beguiled by pledges of better living conditions at a time when it was hard to imagine that conditions could be worse. Mao Tse-tung promised a stable economy.
Chiang Kai-shek, as the hon. member knows, had driven the communists into one small section of China. He also knows that General Marshall, by calling a truce between the nationalist government and the communists, permitted the Chinese communists to be rearmed and helped by Russia. They became a tower of strength in the north, and then when Chiang Kai-shek did not receive the necessary military assistance, when his soldiers were falling away because they had no munitions, or not the right kind of munitions, the communists drove him to Formosa. How could anyone defend a great territory like China against an enemy who was so well supplied with equipment, and, I must say, well led?
There is another article I think I ought to mention in this magazine the China Monthly, at page 288, written by Colonel W. Bruce Pirnie, of the United States Air Force, and entitled "Who Hamstrings U.S. Military Aid to China?" That article was written in 1948,

External Affairs
as late as the month of October that year. It is stated that on April 3 the United States congress had appropriated $125 million for aid to China, and yet by early autumn nothing had been shipped. That does not look as if billions had been spent in a hurry.
In what year?

This was in 1948, and the article goes on to analyse 60,000 tons of war munitions that were sent to China, of which only 2.1 per cent were of any value. The rest of it was useless. It was not the kind of ammunition that they needed. This is the sort of thing that gave rise to a lot of people complaining that China was being betrayed within the state department of the United States. Many people have said the same thing since.
The hon. member also made reference to reactionary regimes like that of Syngman Rhee in South Korea. I wonder what sort of regime my hon. friend wants to have in Korea? He links Chiang Kai-shek with Syngman Rhee. I believe one must remember that these countries have not the tradition of representative and responsible government in the same way that we have. We have a long tradition going back almost a thousand years in this form of government. Neither the Chinese nor the Koreans have had that sort of government. I believe it is a credit to their intelligence that they have been willing to accept our form of government and try to get along with it. I think we must make allowances for the fact that it is a novel experiment; with time and patience they should be able to do something for their country.
The hon. member also said that probably Russia helped to arm the Chinese. I am sure he did not need to put in that word "probably". The probability is so great that I think he could speak with moral certitude on that point. The Chinese communist government had no one else to look to for any kind of financial or military assistance. It was from Russia that she received assistance, partly in the form of Japanese equipment and partly in the form of Russian equipment. He says that a large part of their armour came from our country, and had been delivered into their hands by the Chinese soldiers of Chiang Kai-shek. I do not think it is necessary to make any further reference to that.
Then he went on to say that China never will be controlled by an outside nation. The nationalists in China are in retreat. They are on Formosa. Probably in my hon. friend's opinion they do not count for much at the present time. But I would remind him that

the Netherlands government retreated, that the French government retreated and that Chiang Kai-shek retreated before from the Japanese. There is a possibility-it may be a miracle, but let us pray for this miracle to happen-that the Chinese nationalists, the true friends of the western nations, will be able to redeem the territory that has been lost to the communists. We must remember this tragic fact. China controlled by the communists is China controlled by Russia, by a foreign government. My hon. friend says that he inclines to the view that China will develop an independence of its own, something like that of Tito in Yugoslavia- I believe that is the fervent wish of my hon. friend-and that perhaps they may behave themselves as civilized human beings. But does the record up to the present time show that? I refer to the record of the massacres of which we hear, of the confiscations of which we hear, and of the imprisonments of innocent and holy people of which we hear. According to the bulletin of the SS. Peter and Paul missionaries, quoted in the Catholic Digest, the issue of April, 1952, here is what we find:
Bed China
Chinese prisons now hold 22 bishops, at least 400 priests and about 100 sisters. Since the communist regime began two years ago, missionaries forced to leave China number more than 1,500. About 1,000 foreign missionaries remain, including priests and nuns, plus 1,000 Chinese priests, next target of the Reds.
We have a tyranny in China and it is not to be passed over as just a mere minor affair; it is an international affair. The Chinese communists are doing in China what the communists did in Russia, what they did in Poland and what they did in any country over which they have been able to gain control.
I want to draw to the attention of the house another article. This is one which appeared in the March issue of the Catholic Digest, quoting the views of Archbishop Paul Yu-Pin, the archbishop of Nanking. This is a man who owns six dailies and two radio broadcasting stations in China. This will accentuate what I have already said as to how terrible is the situation in which we now find ourselves. We do not actually realize how serious the situation is. He says:
If China is written off as lost to communism, the whole of Asia will then soon fall. Save China, and you save Asia. If Asia is lost to the communists, lost with its vast storehouse of material resources and almost unlimited reservoir of manpower, can anyone doubt that, within our time, the communists will dominate the world? We are today witnessing the appearance of the real Yellow Peril.
Order. The hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker,
I rise to take part in this debate with some diffidence. In spite of the outstanding contributions which have been made by many of the hon. members who have preceded me,
I feel that there are one or two points on which useful comment may still be made.
I am convinced that the salient fact that we should keep before us at the present time, and in this debate, is that we are now passing through an extremely critical period in world affairs and that, if we are to go through this period without disaster, we must approach the problems which are before us with a clear and a calm understanding and an almost detached view.
After the end of the second world war we in the western world passed quickly through the stage which we might call the stage of popular recognition of the danger of international communism. The phrase "our gallant Russian allies" quickly lost its meaning under the impact of a series of melancholy and unhappy events in eastern Europe and in Asia. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), who has just taken his seat, has referred to some of those events which took place in the Far East. As the result of this awakening of public realization of danger, those of us who had always recognized atheistic communism for what it is-the most dangerous and the most insidious international conspiracy and also, I think, the most brutal and imperialistic dictatorship that the world has ever known- were gradually joined by, I believe, a large and preponderating majority of the rightthinking people of the western world.
The result of this realization of danger was that the western nations embarked on a great program of self-defence. They embarked on the difficult task of turning from the hopes and the desires of peace to the building up of their collective strength for defence. The main instruments through which this program has been carried on are the Atlantic pact and, under it, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Before I conclude, I should like to say something with respect to that particular phase. Before that, however, I should like to say that from some points of view it is almost fantastic to refer to as success what has already been achieved; but from other points of view great forward strides have been made and the success that has been achieved has, I believe, brought us into a second stage and one which presents great dangers of its own. That is the stage at which the success which we are achieving in providing for our defence against aggression may give rise to a false sense of security which will not
External Affairs
only hinder the progress of our present program but might at the worst undo all the good which has already been done.
In such circumstances I think there is a duty on all those who believe that the danger from communist aggression is not past, so to state their belief and to state it without any equivocation or without any reservation whatsoever. For those who are in a position to do so it is also a duty to counteract, with the recounting of sober and unpleasant facts, *the work which communist propaganda is trying to do throughout the world today, namely to build up in the free world a false feeling of security. I believe it is this fact which renders important the divergence of views which has become apparent both inside and outside this house between the thinking and the policies of the Liberal party and this government on the one hand, and those of the C.C.F. party on the other.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), in dealing with certain policy statements of the C.C.F. and statements made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), did not suggest that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was a communist. I think that the hon. member was correct, in his references to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs had said, in saying that he was not required to defend himself against a charge of communism. In fact the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not call him a communist. What the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, as I heard and read his words- and said quite properly-was that the views of the C.C.F. party as officially expressed, both in this house and outside of it, come dangerously close to the present line of the communist party. I think-and I am sure *that many will agree with me-that the adoption by Canada, or by other countries of the western world, of the policies which are being advocated by the C.C.F. would be regarded by the Russians as a victory and a forward step, from their point of view. I feel that the Secretary of State for External Affairs had an absolute duty to point out this danger and to express himself in the *terms and in the sense that he did.
This division of view, Mr. Speaker, proceeds very largely on the question of the importance and the necessity of economic aid and economic development within the western world, as opposed to the development of our immediate defence build-up. The hope and ideal of giving economic aid and assistance to underdeveloped countries, and to contribute to the rehabilitation of Europe, have a tremendous appeal to all Canadians. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it has its

External Affairs
greatest appeal to the Liberal party, and to the supporters of the Liberal party, because this party has, in the domestic sphere, such an outstanding record of achievement in the field of economic development and social betterment, as opposed to the record of talk about economic improvement and social betterment, which is virtually the sole boast of parties opposite.
However, Mr. Speaker, no matter how attractive the possibility of real economic aid may be, it is our duty to attend to our defence, and we must provide for our mutual security and the defence of freedom, liberty and justice as a first call upon our resources and our ingenuity.
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), in the course of his remarks, moved an amendment to the present motion, which provides for a censuring of this government for not laying more stress on the performance of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty. Article 2 of the treaty reads as follows:
The parties will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and well-being. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
I have read article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty because I think that the reasons for voting against and defeating this amendment have already been clearly put on the record in this debate by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his opening speech, and by the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his very able speech, dealing with the measures which are being taken on the economic side. I consider, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian government is putting the right emphasis on both features of our external policy at the present time. I hope, and I am sure that this hope is shared by all hon. members, that as the international situation improves in the future this emphasis may properly and gradually be shifted towards more constructive action in the economic field. However, at the present time we must keep before us the prime objective of ensuring first of all our security and the protection of our allies in the western world.
I should like to mention a few points arising out of the speech delivered in this debate by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). We always enjoy listening to the hon. member, and we listen to him with great attention and respect. However, I should like to quote what the hon. member for Peel had to say 
at page 675 of Hansard, in referring to the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
I thought that at one stage he sounded a rather hostile, and certainly a rather provocative note that, to my mind, was not justified in the circumstances. I hope he did not mean his words to be provocative; but, having in mind the fact that very recently he has been in another quarrel with another party in the house, I was wondering if he thought that perhaps he ought to even up the score, and suggest that some academic discussion should take place on some matters in connection with the Far East.
Then at page 677 he had this to say:
It is all very well for the minister and the government to say they are watching vigilantly to see how many people on this side of the house are going to support them in their Far Eastern policies and so on. Why, you would think he was trying to catch some of the people off guard on some of these academic questions. Instead of that, if I may say so, the minister should be recognizing his own responsibility for the confusion that exists in the public mind right across Canada.
I presume that in using those words the hon. member for Peel was referring to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in his opening remarks at page 662, as follows:
On this question, Mr. Speaker, the policy of the government is clear. I hope that before this debate is finished the position of the official opposition, and of the other opposition parties, will also be made clear. We should know where we stand on these matters, and I hope that it will be shown that at least on essentials, and on principles, we stand together.
That is apparently the invitation that was characterized by the hon. member for Peel as an invitation to academic debate, and by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) as an invitation to schoolboy debate. It is my view that the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which I have quoted, is one that he had a duty to make and it is one that the leaders of the opposition parties have a duty to adopt, giving a clear statement of their policies.
The hon. member for Peel referred to confusion in the public mind. He may be correct that there is some confusion in the public mind on matters of external policy, but I believe that any confusion that does exist is not as to the government's position, but as to the position of the critics of the government. The succession of extremely clear and surprisingly detailed statements which have been made by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs have placed the Canadian public in a very good position to determine easily what the policy of the government is on almost every important question in external matters that is facing this country at the present time. But I would very much doubt whether very many numbers of the public would be able to read the speech of the hon.

member for Peel and get any clear conception of what the policy of the Progressive Conservative party is on one or more of these very important problems. For example, the hon. member for Peel himself had this to say at page 674 of Hansard. Here he is speaking about the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and he said:
But right at this moment, if I say nothing else with respect to our position in this debate, I wish to make it abundantly clear-and perhaps there is no need for us to make it clear-that at this time we feel strongly that the emphasis must be laid on and the urgent priority given to military preparedness and rearmament; because only behind a wall of military security can these other desirable objectives be achieved.
I think we should welcome that statement from the hon. member for Peel, but the phrase to which I should like to direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, is his statement that apparently he is afraid that nothing else regarding the position of his party will be clear as a result of his speech. I am very much afraid he was correct in that estimate of what he proposed to say. I feel therefore that if there is any confusion in the public mind in Canada the responsibility of the government with regard to that confusion is very small indeed. A real effort has been made to place matters of importance before the Canadian people, and to place them in a position to come to informed and reasonable conclusions about the matter.
However, there have been a great many statements from the other side of the house by spokesmen of opposition parties, which have been generally critical of the government's position, but have not dealt as fully as they should have with the points of view of those particular parties. The confusion, if it exists at all, is as a result of the failure of the opposition parties to make clear the points in respect of which they disagree with present government policy.
There is one thing however for which I think we ought all to be thankful, and that is that all parties in the house appear to be agreed on the necessity for the Atlantic pact, and our supporting the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The support of that position, as voiced by the C.C.F. party, is subject to very grave reservations-
Name the reservations.
-and some people may feel that the reservations are more important than the support. I hope that is not so.
Name the reservations.

The hon. member has listened to the speeches of the hon. member for
External Affairs
Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and he knows the reservations as well as I do. But if there are no reservations, then I trust the hon. member, or some other member of his group, will make that abundantly clear. That is all I am asking.
Canada should feel a great sense of pride in the initiative she has taken in the formation of the Atlantic pact and North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I remember very well indeed on a September evening in 1947 hearing over the radio a rebroadcast of a speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who was then secretary of state for external affairs, and the leader of the Canadian delegation at the assembly of the United Nations. On that occasion he made a speech on behalf of Canada before the first plenary session of that assembly, and it was in that speech that the first public expression was given to the necessity and advisability of a treaty being concluded between the United States and the rest of the western world which, in time, became the Atlantic pact.
I remember the sincerity with which that speech was made and the realization I had afterwards that what had been suggested was something that held great possibilities for world peace, and for the unification of all those countries having similar ideals and purposes. I think that in the years that have passed since then we have all felt a great sense of pride that this Atlantic pact has become a reality and that it is recognized not only throughout the western world but in the communist world as well as largely a Canadian achievement. We must feel pride when we realize that to a great extent this has been the result of Canadian thought and initiative, and Canada's determination to cooperate with all like-minded countries in the establishment of a lasting peace.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to follow the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey). During the course of his speech he said that the C.C.F. had certain reservations about NATO. I think I asked him at least three or four times to tell me what the reservations were, or to tell the house, and he was either unwilling to do so or incapable of doing so. I suggest that the latter reason is probably the correct one.
Our position with regard to NATO is very clear-cut and very well known. We support NATO as it is at present constituted without any reservations whatsoever. But we do say this, that the government of this country-

This is number one.

External Affairs

We do say
that the government, by its inaction in helping the nations of Europe economically, is contributing to what might be unhappily the ultimate success of the communists. That is the thing we oppose; and because we oppose it we insist there must be more sacrifice on the part of Canadians to defeat communism in Europe, by means of economic help. If that is a reservation, then my hon. friend is welcome to call it that.
Either the hon. member or someone else stated that the policy of the C.C.F. in regard to our position in NATO is dangerously close to the line of the communist party. That is unadulterated nonsense. We want to see NATO strengthened, but we do believe that the way to strengthen it is by giving still more economic aid to those countries in Europe which are our allies, so that they may be able to withstand the economic menace.
I regret that I was not able to follow directly after the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), yet perhaps it is just as well, because he would have distracted me somewhat from what I was going to say. But I can assure him of this. I am happy he is not responsible for writing the history books of this country of ours. Having listened to him quote Kohlberg and others of the China lobby, I can only hope he is one of the last reactionaries in his party.
In so far as the debate proper is concerned, it was manifestly impossible for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to have included during the course of his speech a reference to every sore spot in the world. He did make passing reference to Indo-China, and then went on to other matters. I wish he had dealt at greater length with the situation there, because I feel now, as I did two years ago, that the potential dangers in Indo-China are even greater than they are in Korea.
There are other areas also upon which he might elucidate further at a later time. I agree however with the hon. member for Halifax in his reference to the reply by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) when the Secretary of State for External Affairs addressed certain quite pointed questions to that hon. member. It is not good enough to say that one regards a debate on what is happening in Asia as something academic. What is happening today in Korea is certainly not academic. What is happening in Indo-China is far from academic. And our policy toward China is also something which cannot be put into the academic category.

I disagree again with the hon. member for Peel when he says that our policy in the Far East should be almost on a day to day basis. That, I think, would be folly. We have to have a long term policy. We have to know why we are pursuing a policy in which we believe, and where we hope to get with it.
The minister has made it reasonably clear as to what our policy is in respect to certain areas in Asia. We are not prepared, he said, to give assistance to Chiang Kai-shek; we are not prepared to help him back to the mainland; we have no desire to destroy the regime in Peking, no matter how much we may happen to dislike it.
We can only hope these policies are made abundantly clear to the Chinese administration. We can only hope that policies similar to those above which have been stated in the capitals of other western countries have been made clear to China, although I doubt if that is so. The Chinese are still obviously suspicious of the west, and perhaps with good reason when we remember the fulminations of MacArthur, and when we listen to Admiral Fechteler when that gentleman says that the Korean war should be carried to the Chinese coast, if no armistice can be signed in Korea.
Statements such as these given by people in responsible positions surely only make the task which we have more difficult. I am convinced we are not going to achieve any political settlement in Korea until we have a peaceful settlement with China. And when I speak of peace I regard it in the same way as Litvinoff did at the league of nations a number of years ago when he said that peace is indivisible. We cannot be at peace with China in Korea and at war with China in Formosa.
And so we shall have to have a general settlement of the Asian problem, if that is possible, before we can achieve peace in Korea. But what the Chinese fear is that if peace is arrived at in Korea, then the Americans may be tempted to transfer their troops from fighting in Korea to the support of Chiang Kai-shek in Formosa.
The first and obviously the most important step we have to take is to achieve a truce. General Ridgway, speaking the other day, asked the western world once again to be patient and to realize the difficulties which confronted the negotiators. I think we have been patient, I think we do realize the difficulties that are there. But speaking of the armistice talks, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is reported on page 664 of Hansard of March 22 as follows:
They take the form of offensives and counteroffensives, attacks and counter-attacks, and it is impossible to be either optimistic or pessimistic about an eventual satisfactory conclusion.

I think those who are conducting the negotiations for us in Korea should be satisfied not to indulge any longer in counter-offensives or counter-attacks. I remember a few weeks ago the Chinese advanced a proposition concerning a peaceful settlement of the Korean situation which ended with the words "et cetera." For three or four days there was discussion as to precisely what the words "et cetera" meant. Admiral Joy said at one time, and I have no way of knowing whether he carried his point or not, that et cetera certainly did not include Formosa. That was a political decision which it was not for the military to make. If the substituting of civilians for the group at present carrying on negotiations will bring about a truce sooner, then I think it would be worth while to make that substitution, no matter whose toes may be trod upon in the process.
It is with the signing of the truce that new difficulties and new problems will appear. One unhappy fact that has come out is that no potential leader seems to have appeared in Korea since the war started. There may be a very good reason for that. If he appeared in North Korea he would be liquidated as a reactionary; if he appeared in South Korea he would be destroyed as a communist collaborator. That is one of the unhappy facts we have to face. Above all we have to leave the Koreans to their own future without any western interference. They may not have the sort of government we would like to see there, but that is their business and not ours.
The devastation and destruction that has been wrought in that country is almost beyond comprehension. Over 15 per cent of the population, over 15 per cent of the men, women and children, are dead. One hundred thousand children are wandering up and down Korea without any future or hope. Five million people are displaced. Three-quarters of a million homes have been destroyed and there are so many maimed that the number cannot be counted. There are so many maimed that a United Nations committee has decided to build a factory in Korea for the manufacture of artificial limbs. I should like to give the house just one example of the many countless tragedies which today are taking place in Korea. This is from a book called "The Korean Reporter" written by Rene Cutforth, a BBC correspondent in Korea. Dealing with the effects of napalm, he has this to say:
In front of us a curious figure was standing, a little crouched, legs straddled, arms held out from his sides. He had no eyes, and the whole of his body, nearly all of which was visible through tatters of burnt rags, was covered with a hard black
External Affairs
crust speckled with yellow pus. A Korean woman by his side began to speak, and the interpreter said:	"He has to stand, sir, cannot sit or lie."
He had to stand because he was no longer covered with a skin, but with a crust like crackling which broke easily.
No one can think of what we are doing there without being filled with a sense of spiritual desolation. But we are at war. No one can think of what we are doing there to the innocent and guiltless without a feeling of almost infinite compassion. But still we are at war. Napalm is a terrible weapon, yet I doubt if it is any less worse at times than high explosive. The atom bomb is a fearsome instrument of war, yet I doubt if it is any worse than napalm except in magnitude. Our minds should rise in revolt against the use of these things, but we are at war and we must conclude that war, and conclude it successfully.
That is why I say that the sooner we arrive at a truce, the better. Following upon that, the sooner we can arrive at a settled and reasonable and honest peace, the better. None of us wants to perpetuate these horrors which are taking place, but I repeat that once we arrive at a truce, once we arrive at a peace, we shall have before us the great task of reconstruction which must be carried out without any strings attached. I hope that we will not make again the mistake of becoming Asian Warwicks.
I should like to refer briefly to the situation in Indo-China, which I said earlier is potentially more serious than the situation in Korea. Today the French are growing tired and weary. They are becoming desperate because of the drain upon their resources. I think it is fair to assume that the Viet Minh are also becoming tired of a fight which has been going on since 1946. We do not know the cost to the Viet Minh, but we do know that it is costing France at least one billion dollars a year. Many of the flower of French manhood are being killed. The French are in the position where they would like to bring back the divisions they have in Indo-China to Europe so that they could correct any imbalance which appears there, due to other plans that are being made.
The Viet Minh are getting Chinese help. France has been getting help from the United States and to some extent from Great Britain. The main thing is that on the northern border of Indo-China there is a Chinese army of from one hundred thousand to two hundred and fifty thousand men. We do not know what they are going to do, but I think it is a safe assumption that if military assistance is given to the French in that area in the shape of troops then these Chinese divisions will move from the north. That might be

External Affairs
almost fatal to our hopes of saving Asia from going entirely communist. If the Chinese were to go in there they would control one of the breadbaskets of Asia.
We know that recently the Chinese suffered from a famine. We know that they are not self-sufficient in the matter of rice or other foods. That opens up the possibility that they will look with acquisitive eyes upon Indochina, but if Indo-China goes, so will Thailand and Burma.
That is one reason why I welcome the suggestion made a few weeks ago in Paris by Mr. Schuman. He proposed that the time had come to start negotiating with the Viet Minh in an attempt to bring about peace.
In so far as China is concerned, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) apparently believes implicitly that China controlled by the communists-these are his words-is a China controlled by Russia. I do not believe that the evidence adds up to that. I am still not convinced that China is a soviet satellite. In 1949 Mao said that the Chinese problem must be solved by the Chinese, that they would not tolerate outside interference. That outside interference applied to Russia as well as to the western world.
I have not been in China but I have read something about it and have discussed it with those who have been there. I think it is fair to say that the Chinese still regard foreigners as barbarians. Who can blame them for that? But "foreign barbarians" includes the Russians, and therefore it precludes the possibility of the Chinese regarding Stalin as their master. Indeed when history comes to be written, when we come to get a proper perspective on events, I think we shall find that the Chinese revolution has been as legitimate as was the French revolution. It was a revulsion against misery, a revolution against foreign domination.
It is in the national interest, it is in our highest interest to attempt to achieve with them a peaceful settlement as soon as possible. Otherwise we run the risk pointed out by the hon. member for St. John's West of forcing China into the arms of Russia. On the other hand, if we arrive at a peaceful settlement with the Chinese then they themselves will find that they have their own problems on their own hands.
The hon. member for St. John's West has perhaps forgotten that it was Chiang Kai-shek who handed over Manchuria and Mongolia to the Russians. China wants those provinces back.
Was that as a result of the signing of the Russian treaty with China, the treaty that China was forced to sign?

No, it was
done voluntarily in return for Russian assistance. I want to remind my hon. friend that when Chiang Kai-shek was fighting on the mainland in China he was getting Soviet assistance and the ideological colleagues of Stalin were getting none. That is one of the things which Mao remembers.
What time was that?

About 1947 or 1948. The Chinese want those provinces back because they are wealthy and rich provinces. I suspect that one of the reasons for Mao's going to Moscow was to see what he could do about getting them back. He did not come back with them, but he came back with something which no other nation, certainly no satellite, has emerged with from Moscow. He came back with an agreement which on the face of it was mainly to the benefit of China. Russia promised to withdraw from Dairen and Port Arthur.
Russia promised to give China back certain rail facilities. Russia promised a loan of $300 million in United States dollars spread over a period of five years, and also promised the return of military equipment looted from Manchuria. I have no means of knowing whether or not those promises will be kept. I do know that no satellite has ever come back from Moscow with such great prizes as the Chinese. The Chinese regard Manchuria as important for we all know it contains fabulous wealth. Sinkiang is potentially rich, and the Chinese want to get it back. I have noticed that recently the Russian commissars have been withdrawn from Sinkiang and replaced by Chinese. The Russians are interested in this area because of the uranium deposits which are supposed to be there. China, because she is an ambitious country, quite naturally wants to get back inner and outer Mongolia. I suggest, therefore, that we should leave them to settle their own problems with Russia, and indeed give them every encouragement to do so. We are not going to make any progress in that until peace is negotiated, and that is why I say our greatest interest is to see that peace is achieved. Otherwise, we shall merely compel the Chinese to turn again to the Soviets for still further solace.
Now, there is another matter which I should like to discuss, one which we have brought up before on the floor of this house, and which has been treated with some

scepticism if not an element of derision. I refer to the fact that we believe there is great danger in the present military control over policy. We are not alone in believing that. I have here a statement by an associate justice of the supreme court of the United States, the Hon. William O. Douglas, who I am sure most people will realize is a very sane and responsible citizen. The heading on this article is, "We Have Become Victims of the Military Mind." I should like to quote part of it:
Some say that although there has been a great inroad of military men into public office, the situation is saved by the umbrella of civilians that is held over them. It is true that many departments, manned by the military, have civilian heads. But anyone who knows government knows that policy is made at the expert level. The hidden layer of military personnel shapes the thinking and policy of many an agency; the civilian heads by and large are merely spokesmen for what the military want. This is a necessary consequence of the complexities of a bureaucracy.
The military have such a dominating influence in our foreign affairs, and foreign affairs are so large in every budget, that military men are inheriting more and more domestic roles.
So states Mr. Justice Douglas, and it is a warning to which we must pay heed. We in the C.C.F. have criticized the United States in the past, and I think it is legitimate to do so when our interests are affected. But that does not in any way reduce by one iota the credit which is due the United States for the generosity it has shown, not only to us but to other nations. When our interests are affected, however, we feel it is legitimate to speak those things which are on our minds as between friends. We look upon the United States as a great and powerful neighbour. We are thankful to have the United States there. But sometimes I think the United States should be very thankful to have a country like Canada on her northern border.
There is evidence to suggest that the joint chiefs of staff in Washington have been making foreign policy. The result has been that we have been presented almost with accomplished facts on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. We had to take it or run the risk of disrupting an alliance which is necessary to our own defence. We do not like that sort of presentation of policy. In May, 1950, General Bradley appeared before the foreign affairs committee and he said then that the rearming of Germany was vital to the defence of the west. That was the opinion of the joint chiefs of staff in May, 1950. We can remember that Europe was thrown into a tailspin by the remarks of the general, and then in September, 1950, we remember Mr. Acheson announcing to the North Atlantic council that the United States favoured rearming Germany. The Secretary of State for External
External Affairs
Affairs will appreciate, I think, the many complications which followed upon that statement by the United States.
It is the policy of the joint chiefs of staff, and they have made it known, to strengthen Chiang Kai-shek in Formosa. Apparently the state department has gone along, and the question is, if the worst comes to the worst, how far are we going to be brought into this whole unhappy imbroglio. It was the joint chiefs of staff who urged that the United States negotiate with Franco to get air bases in Spain, as they became important to their global strategy. The demands of global strategy again may have prompted the joint chiefs of staff to say to the United States that Greece and Turkey should be brought into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I do not know whether or not that is right, but there is reason for believing it to be so. These countries were brought in. Of course, there is military influence, and we must expect it, but we have to be on the watch to see that it does not exceed its legitimate bounds.
There are other areas, too, where it can be felt, if not seen. We have a new administration in the United States, the mutual security administration, which is a single centralized agency under Mr. Averell Harri-man. It is responsible for carrying out military assistance and giving foreign aid. Apparently, it is completely under the control of Mr. Harriman, but unhappily in practice it is the Pentagon which determines the nature of the military aid. The objective behind this administration is to strengthen the economies of assisted countries by increasing their capacity to produce the things which they need. It is a very laudable objective and one which we support. Yet I understand that the French have developed a prototype of one of the most powerful tanks in the world. However, they are not allowed to make it because the United States says that it would take too long to tool-up and get into production. And so tanks are made in the United States and sent to France. Unfortunately, they are not forthcoming in the volume in which the French would like. The British want to make a certain type of helicopter. They were told by the United States: "No, we think we can do it better because we have the facilities and the raw materials." Instead of the European countries getting dollars for manufacturing these things and selling them, they are without the dollars to buy the raw materials which our country has. They are being left not only without the dollars but without the weapons which they need. I think it is most desirable and essential that we rationalize, so far as possible, the production of material amongst the North Atlantic

External Affairs
countries. We are not going to achieve it in this way. It would be advisable to some extent to let each country make that thing which it is competent to make.
This brings me back to the point we raised earlier in this debate, the necessity for economic aid. I take it for granted that hon. members realize the tremendous benefits which United States generosity has conferred upon Europe with the $12 billion of Marshall aid. The people of the United States were more than generous, and they achieved their objective. In 1947 starvation was haunting Europe. Four years later agricultural production had been raised about 95 per cent, industrial production had reached many of its objectives, and maximum output was being achieved. Europe was almost on its feet. Then, the best laid schemes of mice and men really went a-gley, and there was aggression in Korea. The effect of that aggression on the economies of our European allies was almost catastrophic. There was a scramble for raw materials. Naturally those nations which had the dollars had the advantage in the scramble on the markets of the world. The nations of Europe could not afford the new prices. They had to pay more for the materials and therefore they had to export more. By exporting more, they reduced their own standard of living in the search for more dollars. Prices were increased and production fell. Today we see a situation in Europe where the economies of many countries, if not in a dangerous situation, are at least exceedingly shaky. One of the things we object to is that we are building on top of this shaky foundation a huge superstructure, a superstructure of military might, one which is necessary for defence. Unless we have a firm base underneath, it may topple over and crash. Europe needs economic assistance as much as it needs military assistance today. That is our opinion, and it is the opinion of General Gruenther, who was speaking before the senate foreign relations committee a few days ago.
A headline in the Christian Science Monitor says, "Gruenther says Economic Aid is as Vital as Arms," That is one thing to which we have not been paying attention. Ever since I came to parliament in 1945, we in the C.C.F. have argued that the best way to defeat communism in this world is not by guns but by feeding people, and by so raising their standards of living that communism will have no appeal for them. Ours were voices crying in the wilderness, but I am glad to recall that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs came to this
house he also took up the cry. We in the C.C.F. believe we can afford to give more than we have been giving. It has not been very much. This is not original because a friend of mine told it to me, but sometimes I think we are in the position of a man pressing up to the bar amongst the bigger boys to get his share of what is going on, yet when his turn to pay came he beat a very discreet retreat.
Of course we shall be told a week next Tuesday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he comes to this house that everything in Canada is for the best in this best of all possible Canadas-we shall be told that our industrial production is at its peak and our agricultural production is high, and that we are enjoying a high degree of prosperity. If that is so, surely we are able to give more than the small amount we have done in giving economic aid to our allies in Europe. It is possible that the Minister of Finance may be one of those honest souls of whom his leader spoke, one of those honest souls who do not realize the need for further sacrifice. The Minister of Finance may be one of those who do not realize the need for further deprivation if we are going to maintain our national and our collective security. We argue that the purpose of our amendment is to bring forward this fact.
We do not believe that enough is being done by Canada in the fight against communism. The parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his interesting speech yesterday made some excellent and valid points. We are doing apparently as much as we can in the Colombo plan. In the matter of technical assistance, again, we are doing everything we can. But that is not to say that we are doing everything we can in so far as Europe is concerned. I think we should also remember this. We in the C.C.F. are suggesting giving more economic aid to Europe now in the shape of raw materials and those supplies which they need to produce for themselves. We ourselves have been in receipt of economic help, not directly but indirectly. We obtained a billion and a quarter American dollars under Marshall aid, which we badly needed, in the shape of offshore purchases. That aid helped our agriculture and industry substantially.
We are not being deprived of much in this country. We can have guns and butter. But in Europe the problem is guns or bread. When you get that situation communism becomes dangerous. In the last national election in France, despite the gerrymandering of the voters list, 26 per cent of the French voted communist. In the last municipal elections

in Italy, 37 per cent of the people voted communist. There is your greatest threat today. We should therefore do everything which it is humanly possible to do in order to get rid of this threat. The only way to do it is to raise the European standard of living, to raise European production by giving them these raw materials which they need and which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) refused when he was asked by the temporary council committee. The temporary council committee put up a proposition to Canada that we give X number of dollars in aid and raw materials to Europe; whether you put it at $100 million or $200 million at the moment does not matter. I at least will compromise for $100 million. I argue that it would pay us to give Europe today $100 million worth of raw materials. But the answer of the Minister of Finance, this honest soul who has lulled himself into a sense of security, says: Oh, no, we cannot do that; we do not have the dollars. Of course we could get $100 million if we wanted to do so. I told him how to do it the other day. All he has to do is to cut out luxury travel in the United States. But so far as this honest soul who is at the head of treasury is concerned, dollars at the moment mean much more than defence.
Time after time the Secretary of State for External Affairs has come to this house and said: we can help to combat communism with economic aid; and time after time the government has refuted his suggestion by doing nothing. This is an amazing example of governmental schizophrenia. Who is making government policy? Is it the minister who very rightly says that if we are to combat communism we must give economic aid, or is it the Minister of Finance who says that we are not prepared to give anything? I think it is time we know precisely what the situation is. As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said the other day in Toronto:
The foundations of combined strength we have already laid in the free world have given us a greater sense of security and grounds for hope that the war all decent people dread can be prevented. 1 regret to say the precautions we have taken seem to have lulled some honest souls in our midst into a false sense of security, and to have induced them to join in agitation against the sacrifices and deprivations without which we cannot have any security.
Mr. Speaker, the honest souls who refuse to aid our own security are a government who refuse economic aid to our allies when they need it so desperately.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate, certainly not as an expert on international affairs but rather from the point of view of a western Ontario member who had the privilege of
External Affairs
attending the sixth session of the general assembly at Paris last fall. Like the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), and the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), I wish to express my appreciation to the government for my inclusion in the Canadian delegation, which proved to me to be a broadening and educational experience indeed.
The policy of the government in selecting members of the House of Commons and of the Senate as delegates, alternate delegates and observers at the sessions of the United Nations general assembly has my full endor-sation. Such experiences are bound to widen the base upon which a member of parliament has to make up his own mind not only on international issues but on domestic problems as well. To hear Mr. Vishinsky or Mr. Katz-Suchy in one of their tirades is a different matter altogether from reading those gentlemen's speeches in the press. Our policy of sending representatives of opposite political parties as observers at the UN stands out in refreshing relief from the type of representation from the cominform countries.
I wish to report that Canada's prestige at the United Nations is extremely high. It was my honour to represent our country on the sixth or legal committee. On the very first morning we met, a great many delegates from other countries told me how highly Canada was regarded not only at the United Nations but in their respective countries; and as I looked around, I could see that this was not a routine performance. I am sure that other members who have attended previous sessions of the general assembly will confirm the fact that one of the first impressions a newcomer has at the United Nations is of the popularity of Canada and the esteem in which our country is held.
Canada's popularity at the United Nations, I suggest, stems from various reasons: our participation in two world wars; our foreign policy; our assistance to underprivileged countries; and last but not least, the two men who have most recently held the office of secretary of state for external affairs and who headed the Canadian delegations at the United Nations. I did not have the privilege of attending the general assembly when the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) headed the Canadian delegation, but I think all hon. members are fully aware of the extent to which Canada's place in international affairs was enhanced by his leadership and by his subsequent contribution to the creation and development of NATO.

External Affairs
A journey to Paris was not necessary for me to learn the standing of our present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) at the United Nations. His chairmanship of the first or political committee on two occasions, his chairmanship of NATO, and the widespread acclaim he received when his name was mentioned for the position of secretary-general of NATO are known to all hon. members. It was not by mere chance that Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Pearson were nominated recently for the Nobel peace prize.
As you may know, the Secretary of State for External Affairs represented Canada on the first or political committee; the hon. member for Levis represented our country on the second or economic committee and also on the fifth or budgetary committee; Mrs. R. J. Marshall, LL.D., of Agincourt, the immediate past-president of the Canadian Council of Women, on the third or social and humanitarian committee; the hon. member for Kindersley and the Hon. Senator Hurtubise on the fourth or trusteeship committee. The hon. member for Nanaimo was the parliamentary observer for the Progressive Conservative party and while we on this side of the house certainly do not agree with everything he has said since he returned from Paris, I must admit that he was an exceedingly congenial and competent observer.
As many in the house have not had an opportunity of meeting Mrs. Marshall, I want to record the fact that she was a very able delegate. Competing with such notables as Mrs. Roosevelt and Madame Figueroa of Chile, Mrs. Marshall held her own and made many worth-while contributions to the work of our delegation and the third committee. In fact, Canadian women were prominent at the United Nations. Besides Mrs. Marshall, Mrs. Adelaide Sinclair was again elected to the head of UNICEF, the international children's emergency fund. Another prominent Canadian woman was Miss Marjorie Gordon, of the Canadian consulate general of New York, who acted as our press information officer. The work of Miss Gordon, who is the daughter of Ralph Connor, the famous Canadian writer, was outstanding.
Each of the Canadian representatives on the various committees had the benefit of the advice and experience of one or more specialists from the departments of external affairs and of finance. These civil servants impressed me greatly, not only from the point of view of their knowledge and background-they were Rhodes scholars, postgraduates of Oxford and so on, as well as

being veterans of world conferences-but also because they were down to earth practical Canadians.
In order to save money the Department of External Affairs used the services of a number of their personnel who were already stationed in Europe. One of these, Mr. Thomas Stone, our ambassador to Sweden, was given the high honour of being elected chairman of the budgetary committee.
Having spent some time in Paris, I would be remiss if I did not mention General Vanier, our ambassador to France, and his charming wife, who do a tremendous job of selling Canada in France. Their many courtesies to us in Paris made the work of our delegates much easier.
I shall mention only briefly the proceedings of the legal committee. My first thoughts of the legal committee, I must confess, were that it would be difficult for sixty lawyers from sixty countries speaking a variety of languages to reach an agreement on anything. While some of my fears were well founded, generally speaking our discussions proceeded in a satisfactory manner and they were freer from acrimony than those of the other committees. Nine items were assigned to the legal committee, the most important being a proposal to improve the general assembly methods of procedure for dealing with legal and drafting questions, the draft declaration on the rights and duties of states and reservations to the genocide convention and to multilateral conventions.
A great number of items have been covered in this foreign affairs debate and I intend to mention only a few points that have been raised in previous speeches. This is only the second time during the life of this parliament that we have witnessed a motion of lack of confidence in the external affairs policy of our government, the other time being when the C.C.F. party moved an amendment in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last year. Canadians have always prided themselves on the fact that when the chips are down we present a common front to the enemy. Like the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), some of us attended the session of the chamber of deputies in France, at a time when the whole foreign policy of the Pleven government, including France's participation in NATO, was under bitter debate. On that occasion the government was sustained by a very slim majority and I remember our smug thoughts to the effect: "It could not happen at home." I am not suggesting that it is happening to that extent

here, but I must confess that the C.C.F. amendment concerns me, certainly not on its merits, but on the fact that it was moved at all.
This is the second time within the last two weeks that the C.C.F. party has flared up against the government's foreign policy. In moving his amendment the hon. member for Melfort stated that Canada was not contributing a cent to the economic support of her NATO allies. The Secretary of State for External Affairs then asked if the hon. member considered $300 million being voted in our estimates for mutual aid this year as an aid to our NATO partners. The hon. member then said, as recorded at page 771 of Hansard:
"The minister is talking about mutual aid. We are asking that it be extended, not that the insurance be dropped."
I do not know what the hon. member means, but I am not alone in that, because I noticed an editorial in a Toronto morning newspaper and the editor did not know what the hon. member for Melfort meant.

May I enlighten the hon.
member?
Yes.
If he will read clause 2 and clause 3 of the NATO treaty he will find that clause 2 has to do with economic aid, and clause 3 has to do with mutual aid, which are two different things.

Thank you. I think the hon. member for Melfort is getting very legal. I suggest to him that because the words "mutual aid" are mentioned in article 3 and not mentioned in article 2 does not mean that mutual aid cannot strengthen the economies of our allies. I also say to him that just because the President of the United States happened to set aside in his appropriation three different items, it does not mean that we cannot lump ours in one. NATO is one military effort; it is not split up into a number of separate compartments. I say to the hon. member for Melfort, if he has a dollar in his pocket and he decides to buy a book, and I give him that book, he can then go out and buy some other article with that dollar. By giving him the book have I not strengthened his economy, no matter whether I call it mutual aid or economic collaboration?
Let us take a practical example. Let us take the proposition that the French government has decided to provide some money for jeeps which are needed for the defence of France, and we find that in Canada we can make these jeeps more economically, which is true, and under mutual aid we then decide
External Affairs
to give the jeeps to France. Is that not an advantageous mutual bargain all the way through? Are we not strengthening the economy of France? Would not that release money for other expenditures in France? Will not that $324 million which is in the estimates at the present time bolster the economies of our NATO allies?
We lawyers are accused of getting technical, but I was surprised at the hon. member for Melfort putting up the artificial argument that, just because mutual aid is mentioned in article 3 and something about strengthening the economies in article 2, aid under either article is not strengthening the economies of our European allies. The C.C.F. party as a rule has never been that technical about their policy. Further, I should like to say to the hon. member for Melfort-I wish he would not go out: Does he not think that, although the high level NATO talks are being conducted necessarily on a secret basis, that all the different ways in which we can help our NATO allies are being constantly reviewed and under constant survey, and that this $324 million has been passed by our allies and will be gratefully acceptable to them?
It should have been given two years ago, instead of now.
You are changing your story now.
I am not changing the story at all. We have had the same story all along.

As far as economic aid is concerned, we in Canada would like to do much more, but the position of the government is that first things come first. It is the first responsibility of this government to restore our defences to the position that we can resist aggression, after which we shall increasingly direct our attention to giving economic aid to our allies. Our policy in the meantime is to give as much aid as possible. I remember reading in the U.S. News and World Report, issued just a month or so ago, which has been quoted quite often in this house, that a military expert said it would not be until midsummer that our defences could be built up in western Europe to withstand an attack by the twenty-five Russian divisions permanently stationed in east Germany and Poland alone, to say nothing about a full-scale attack by the main Russian armies. I can still remember Mr. Vishinsky, and I am sure the hon. member for Melfort remembers him, with his owlish, blinking eyes, wagging his finger at the delegation of the west, and saying: You

External Affairs
are spending too much on armament. He would like very much to have us reduce our expenditures on armaments.

My amendment does not
suggest that we cut down on armaments.

I am not suggesting that the hon. member did suggest that; I am just saying that Mr. Vishinsky would welcome it. I wish every hon. member had the opportunity to see Mr. Vishinsky and Mr. Malik in action. If they had, the debate in this house would proceed on a different line.
Naturally, the whole purpose of this C.C.F. amendment is to create the impression in this country that Canada is not doing its bit. Like the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), I am annoyed. When you go out of Canada you find that the people praise this country for its generosity; when you go to the United Nations the people there keep telling you that this country is at the head of the list, or near the head of the list, in contributing to the international community chest. You come home and then you are confronted with an amendment like the one moved by the hon. member for Melfort. I agree with the hon. member for Cochrane that the C.C.F. party would be the first to complain if taxes were raised to pay for this increased economic assistance that they suggest. Canada after all is only a nation of 14 million people.
The leader of the C.C.F. party referred to the need for an attempt, and a continuous endeavour, to reach a progressive disarmament agreement among the nations, and particularly with Russia. That of course is the policy of our government. To give full credit to the leader of the C.C.F. party, he fully explained in his speech he realized that that is the policy of all the free nations of the world.
At the sixth general assembly every attempt was made by the democratic countries to narrow the gulf between them and the communist world. You will recall that at the very outset, Mr. Dean Acheson, on behalf of the big three, advanced a progressive disarmament program. It was that proposal that Mr. Vishinsky said was so funny he could not get to sleep that night for laughing. Again, in number one committee the same scheme was put forward in more detail. Later a subcommittee of the political committee met in secret, attended only by the representatives of France, United States, the United Kingdom and Russia. Hope was held in some quarters that since the meeting of this subcommittee was to be held behind closed doors, something productive would be the outcome. After all, it is difficult to hold a round-the-table discussion with representatives of sixty

nations in attendance and in the limelight of radio, press and television. So for a whole week an American, an Englishman, a Russian and a Frenchman discussed disarmament, but at the conclusion of the meeting the report of the subcommittee showed the same deadlock existed as had obtained in the political committee and in the general assembly. As had been said on many occasions, the heart of the matter is the refusal of the Kremlin to accept the principle of international inspection and control of arms, including atomic installations. Such inspection and control, according to Russia, interfere with its national sovereignty. It is elementary to say that we of the west cannot agree to disarm, and pursuant to that agreement actually disarm, unless we see for ourselves and know for certain that other countries are doing the same. We cannot gamble our way of life on the word of the Kremlin.
Of course the real heart of the matter is that the Russians are not interested in reaching a genuine agreement on world disarmament and therefore world peace. If such an agreement could be reached, Canada could spend the billions it is now expending for national defence on such things as the development of our natural resources, on social benefits such as national health insurance, and for assistance to the underprivileged nations of the world-the very antithesis of what Mr. Stalin desires.
And so, at the session of the United Nations I attended, the delegates of the U.S.S.R., Byelorussia, the Ukraine, Czechoslovakia and Poland blocked, stalled, raised points of procedure and did everything they could to prevent the nations of the world from reaching an agreement on disarmament and, for that matter, from reaching an agreement on anything. I came to the conclusion it was impossible to have a discussion with communist delegates. Each time such a delegate spoke he delivered a long propaganda speech, always along the same pattern, branding the United States, the United Kingdom and the western democracies, as warmongers, and asserting that Russia alone stood for peace. Even in our legal committee, which enjoyed the reputation of being fairly free from political propaganda, the U.S.S.R. delegate on one occasion told of what he called the start of the Korean war, by describing in fairly great detail the invasion of North Korea by American troops. The Moscow line is even more fantastic to listen to than it is when one reads it in the newspapers.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) mentioned the atmosphere of the United Nations. I can assure him there was

the same atmosphere last fall that he described when he was there some years ago. The iron curtain is still down at the United Nations, so far as Soviet delegates are concerned. These delegates, both in and out of meetings, were always very careful not to earn the reputation of being too friendly with anyone from the west.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) suggested that if Russia were ever to have a genuine turn of heart, because of the mistrust that has been built up throughout the years we might not then recognize Russia's sincerity. Well, my only answer to that is that it is possible, but I do not think it is probable, because the west is longing for peace. It will be recalled that Mr. Vishinsky made a speech last February before the United Nations in which he said that Russia was then willing to accept the principle of continuing inspection. The whole west, even though we had been fooled many times by Mr. Vishinsky's speeches, was filled with hope. Of course two or three days later his speech was analysed and clarified, when he said Russia was willing to accept continuing inspection, so long as it did not interfere with the domestic life of the state. There is always a catch in Mr. Vishinsky's speeches.
I suggest to the hon. member for Acadia that, even so, our policy remains that the door to negotiations will be kept open; not only will it be kept open, but there will be someone there on watch.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar intimated that Canada is gaining quite a reputation at the United Nations for its abstentions. I am not aware of the basis for such a remark, and I certainly do not concur in the suggestion that Canada has gained that reputation. While I was there, any time Canada abstained I was satisfied that we had a good reason for abstaining.
