Undoubtedly there are occasions when, in the interests of our country and of world peace and understanding, it is wise to abstain rather than to cast either an affirmative or a negative vote. As the hon. member must fully realize, Canada does occupy a unique position in world affairs, not only being the go-between and the confidante of Great Britain and the United States, but also being a member of NATO and of the British commonwealth of nations. It is no wonder the statement has often been made that no other 14 millions of people exert the same degree of influence as does the Canadian nation at the conference tables of the world.
I enjoyed the speech of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who has had a great deal of experience in the field of foreign
External Affairs
affairs, and who serves as foreign affairs critic of the Progressive Conservative party. From what I could see, his chief complaint against the policy of the government was that not enough information has been released as to what NATO is doing. All I can say about that is that I agree with the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) in his submission that a good deal of information has been given in this debate both by the minister and by his parliamentary assistant. It is customary of course for the opposition to demand more information, regardless of how much has already been given. During the same debate I mentioned, when I attended in the chamber of deputies in Paris, I noted that the opposition there-and it made me homesick for the Progressive Conservatives-were asking for more information, too. It was denied them on grounds of security. I do not know how the people of Peel county feel, but many of the good people of Grey have told me that they believe democratic countries give out too much information as it is.
Reference has been made in the debate to the fact that, during recent months, many leaders of western countries have expressed the view that the danger of the immediate outbreak of a third world war is lessening. Those opinions, while always expressed in a cautious manner, have undoubtedly encouraged the thinking among some of our people that Russia has no intention of provoking an attack, and therefore we are wasting billions of dollars on national defence. Those same people reason that if Russia had entertained plans for invading Europe or Japan, those plans would have been implemented by now, before the free world had the opportunity to rearm.
Two answers are suggested in reply to that line of thinking: First, Russia has been doing exceedingly well since 1945 in its campaign to dominate the world. Six hundred million people have been added to its empire. We have lost Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Hungary, Roumania and China. It may well be that the Russian campaign is progressing exactly according to the master plan locked up in the Kremlin. And all this has been accomplished without the loss of a Russian soldier.
The second reason for the failure of Russia to take the offensive in an all-out attack may be found in the statement of Mr. Winston Churchill as it appears in British Hansard, of March 5, 1952, where he said:
... I am not suggesting that it is sufficient for our safety in the event of war, and I rely on the rapidly growing and already overwhelming power of the United States in the atomic bomb to provide

External Affairs
tht ueterrents against an act of aggression during the period of forming a defensive front in western Europe.
Then of course there may be other reasons which deter Russia. It may be that Mr. Stalin is fearful of the Tito-inspired type of communism in southeast Europe or it may be that he is mindful of the thousands of Russian soldiers who deserted to the enemy when Hitler invaded the Ukraine. Unfortunately we cannot depend upon any of these reasons; if any of them is held by Moscow, it may disappear overnight in the minds of the men of the Kremlin.
This returns us to the premise, upon which apparently all of us are agreed, that collective security under NATO is a necessity. Banding together for collective security is as old as mankind, starting with the family alliance, progressing to city fortifications, then to the tribe, then to the country and finally to groups of nations. But NATO is one step farther. While combined military activity is almost as old as warfare, never before has military unification been attempted.
Naturally therefore numerous obstacles and difficulties were encountered in setting up NATO, particularly when that organization was so quickly thrown together. While many problems remain, many of the obstacles and difficulties which had appeared on agenda after agenda at NATO meetings were solved at Lisbon. Our minister has warned us that it is one thing to make a decision and another to implement it. But optimism was the keynote at Lisbon-not gloom. A new organization such as NATO-and I say this to the party directly opposite-needs boosting, not knocking.
While NATO is a necessity and will receive our full support as long as it is necessary, we still have faith in the United Nations. In his speech to the general assembly last fall the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
I for one am not prepared to abandon hope of negotiations within the United Nations to ease the present tension.
The principles laid down at San Francisco in 1945 are still the hopes of mankind.
We have been warned it may be a long hard pull, in the struggle against communism. Tremendous tasks confront us. We must continue to give full support to NATO; we must see to it that the United Nations is retained as the hope of mankind; our program of assistance to the underprivileged countries of the world must be increased substantially, as soon as our defences have been built up to the minimum required for survival; meanwhile our home fires, and those of our allies, must be kept burning brightly.

All those tasks, gigantic as they be, are of one pattern. Whether we send an F-86E to Europe, or a carload of wheat to India, we are adding to the temple of peace which free men everywhere are striving to build.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate at a very serious moment when, within the past few hours, an attempt has been made on the life of the West German chancellor. We in this house cannot make the same mistakes in connection with this attempt to build a free Germany as were made when the Weimar republic was allowed to disintegrate and to become destroyed, with the inevitable rise of a dictator.
What I intend to say about Germany certainly will not be popular in many parts of this house, but we must know who are our friends and we must endeavour not to make the mistakes we made before. We must at all costs endeavour to integrate Germany as a full partner with ourselves and the other members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Nothing less will do. There can be no subservient position for Germany. I say this because I believe it is true.
I spent some time over there last year. If there is any country in Europe which today is more aware of the dangers of communism, which is face to face with communist aggression to a greater degree than any other country, it is Germany. All you need to do is to live in western Berlin where the Russians are just across the street. There you will find communism in its greatest strength. You get away from Russian aggression in France, Italy and other countries, but there the communist party, perhaps born of ignorance, is strong.
There appears to be in this house and in all democracies the frightful fallacy that freedom does not have to be fought for. International freedom is not something that comes naturally. Throughout history international freedom has always had to be fought for. Unless we are prepared to fight for international freedom, it will be destroyed. While I regret what is happening to our economy in our effort to provide the necessary arms and military equipment, nevertheless I cannot support the amendment in any way, shape or form because I have seen aggression in action.
Before going on to what I have to say about western Europe I should like to refer to one problem which has been overlooked. Although I have not been brought up to date on this matter by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) or the minister of external affairs, I am interested in knowing what is happening

on the other frontier against communism on the Danube. The frontier against communism in western Europe is to be found in middle Germany, but the other frontier, which is most important, is on the Danube. I hope that in due course this government will appoint a minister to Vienna.
I say that because there is no more active city on the continent of Europe than Vienna in the carrying on of the battle against communism. There is no more courageous government to be found, with the possible exception of the government of Berlin, than the government of Austria. That country is divided and must bear the insufferable occupation of the Russians. Much of the economy of the country is shut off from the western part. But there is no country in Europe which is doing so much today for freedom as the small republic of Austria. I do hope the government will make a statement as to what they propose to do or maybe what they are doing with regard to Austria.
The shape of military aggression in Europe has not been one where mass armies have been used. The Napoleonic wars, the attack in 1914 and the break through in 1940 were all made up of comparatively small numbers of extremely highly mobile forces with tremendous hitting power. If we are to expect aggression, that is the sort of aggression which historically has taken place in Europe.
What we know about Russia's intentions must be changed from month to month, but up to the present there does not seem to be that sort of force being prepared near the western frontier. That may or may not be so in a month's time, but it does not appear that that sort of force is being prepared.
However, we have the unfortunate fact that the potential of the Russian army, both European and Asiatic, is many times that which the western powers could create on a manpower basis. Therefore, if we are to prevent mass creation we must rely more and more on the instruments of war. The mere provision of manpower by a small country like Canada might be dangerous. That manpower has to be backed up by a tremendously increased striking power in the way of weapons of defence. It is regrettable that up until now that has been pitifully small, but that will be the subject of another debate. Weapons, the technical know-how, the ability to destroy the enemy must be an essential part of our Canadian preparedness.
The Russians have another weapon, the weapon of upsetting the economic life of a country by putting the military effort out of balance with the economic production. Today throughout the world the forces of mischief
External Affairs
are blowing in practically every quarter. Markets have been upset, it has been impossible to sell surplus supplies, and in many countries the economy is in grave danger. Therefore, we have to recognize the danger of upsetting the economic life of these countries.
Now, the suggestion put forward of economic aid is, from the humane point of view, perhaps a good thing, but looking at it from the realistic point of view, would it help a Europe today in which you have cartels, embargoes, trade restrictions, customs duties, currency restrictions and every conceivable type of restriction on trade? The Marshall plan and the excellent work that was done under Mr. Hoffman have prevented starvation. They have put the European continent back on its feet. Supposing we had, and I disagree that we have, the wherewithal to provide mass economic aid, would we in any way assist so long as the European continent maintains this system of international economy? In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we would not. The entire production of the North American continent, and, if we could get to it, the nearest fixed star, the entire production of that planet would not aid, so long as these countries will not trade with each other. Just so long as the countries on the European continent continue to set up embargoes against each other, and all these hideous restrictive devices which we have seen since the war, in my opinion nothing is going to save them. I say, therefore, despite the physical aid of the Marshall plan, despite the tremendous help in putting Europe on its feet, restoring plants and the wonderful things that have been done, I do not think you could help Europe without breaking down the economic heresies which are being continued at the present time.
General Eisenhower had something to say on that subject in a press dispatch of a comparatively recent date:
The requirement for a healthy and stable economy in western Europe is not merely of interest for this year or next year. It is a matter of the indefinite future. As time goes on, it seems obvious that it cannot gain strength and stability if it is to remain split up in a number of independent economies. There must be progress towards the unification of western Europe if the objective of permanent security and peace in the western world is to be realized.
That is what the supreme commander says, and he is probably the expert par excellence. His job is to preserve that continent, and he says that unless some integration of the European economy can be brought about- he does not say the job is hopeless, but he

External Affairs
says that the difficulties are tremendous. I quote again from General Eisenhower.
If someone would show me an easier, better answer to the safety and security of the western world, X would certainly be delighted, but I just cannot find it.
I shall add this. I talked to many governmental officials in Europe and I have yet to meet one who ever quarrelled with this theory. Just as long as we do not, politically, economically and in every other way, do everything possible to urge the integration of Europe, we shall not be able to have a prosperous economy on that continent. As long as there is not a prosperous economy, there will not be security. The economy cannot be made prosperous by continuous gifts, whether they are food, money, dollars or anything else. The salvation must come from the European continent.
It seems to me that has been the fallacy in so much of our talk about aid to Europe. The continent is richly endowed with natural resources, yet crisis after crisis takes place in the United Kingdom, in France and in Italy simply because they are trying to make an economic system work which has never worked.
Coming back to Germany, let me say that if we have to fight, we had better have on our side people who we know will fight. We had1 better have on our side people who know what communism is. We had better have on our side people who have experienced communist aggression of their country. Hon. members in this house: Unless you have seen the Russian army in control of a city, unless you have seen what communism can do to a country when it takes over, unless you have seen how that country can be destroyed until not one brick stands upon another, you cannot adequately conceive of the devastation that communism can bring about. Unfortunately, I have seen it. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we had better get people who can fight and who know what they are fighting for.
I had' the privilege last year of talking to a number of men who had been prisoners of war in Russia, who had fought against the Mongolian troops and who had fought outside of Stalingrad. They knew what they were up against. We are not playing for anything but keeps in this game. If we have any overseas policy, it must be to do everything possible to get ourselves allies who will produce and who will fight no matter what we may think about them, no matter what may have happened a few years past, and no matter how barbaric they were some years ago. Today we are fighting for our lives, so let us press forward for the integration of Germany as a full partner. As I have said,
IMr. Adamson.]
we have friends in Germany. We have friends in the German government. By talking appeasement, let us not allow that government to be destroyed. Let us not make the same mistake as we made over the Stresemann government. Let us make sure that the government is shown a co-operative attitude. Let us make every effort we can to strengthen the hand of that government.
Canada is not an occupying power. That fact should be stressed. We are paying for what we eat, I understand, where our troops are billeted in Germany. That fact should be made known. We are there to preserve the peace of Europe. That is all we are there for. We must therefore, in every way possible, make our occupational job as effective as possible. Not only must we provide troops but we must provide technical aid; and we must provide technical aid not only in Germany-because Germany is an extremely highly developed and technical country-but we must provide it elsewhere in the world. The story of Pakistan is an example.
That is how we can help. We can help the peoples of the world grow two blades of grass where one grew before. That can be done through technical aid. It cannot be done by giving them either food or dollars. We may, in an emergency, help out from time to time with famine relief; but that is not the permanent solution. The permanent solution is to have the nations of the world technically able, as far as possible, to produce to save themselves. Because of the very fact of our small population-despite our booming economy at the present time-and because of our peculiar position as a small nation next to a great nation, we cannot afford grandiose expenditures of millions and millions of dollars for aid all over the world. By so doing we destroy our own economy. With a destroyed economy, we can help no one.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word about the Council of Europe in Strasbourg. The name of Briand, whose idea it was, is revered throughout all Europe, with the possible exception of his own native France. That idea, that spark of a united Europe, that spark which somebody called the united states of Europe, that possible dream of a supranational state, is, in my opinion, the best hope for a European community free, economically sound and, above all, secure.
We in this country, in my opinion, can do nothing more helpful in the political field than to aid the Strasbourg assembly, thus aiding the united states of Europe, thus aiding that idea that Briand suggested many years ago, and in every way to do what we can to bring it into being. A divided Europe; a Europe broken up into small, economic

trading units; a small Europe broken up into units with impossible boundaries, with raw materials on the one side and industrial plants on the other side of them, can never be integrated into a unit which will fight and save itself. Unless that result is brought about, we in this country and on the North American continent shall continuously not only have to keep military forces to protect a Europe which cannot protect itself but to have an increasingly large amount of our economy devoted to the wasteful and hateful business of war.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said at the beginning of this debate that he would welcome expressions of opinion from all sides of the house. This debate has gone on now for two or three days, and I think it can be said that the minister has had an expression of opinion from all sides of the house. Whether he agrees with all that has been said, only he knows. But certainly it can be said, and I think truly said, that whatever our differences may be in this debate, we at least agree on one thing, namely, the need for peace in this world. We may differ in the methods by which we achieve or maintain peace, and we may have honest differences about it in this house; but the burning desire of all members, to whatever party they may belong, is peace, and I think the people of Canada should understand that.
Every question which comes up in the world today is dependent on peace. Our economic situation and our social situation depend on whether or not we can maintain peace in this world. I am persuaded that all peoples in this world, including those in Russia, desire peace. Why is it then that we are living in a situation where peace is in jeopardy every hour? The answer to that question should be given here, and in the brief address that I intend to make I shall try to answer it in so far as I am able.
I said last year, and I make no apologies for making the same statement now, that if Russia sincerely desired peace she could have it today, and have it on terms very favourable to her. Why then does she pursue her policy of blocking all efforts for peace? Why does she pursue her propaganda, denouncing our
External Affairs
way of life and our people and our efforts for peace? In my opinion there is only one answer to that, namely, the policy laid down by Lenin, the father of the Russian revolution, when he said that democracy or the free way of life and communism could not live together in this world, and either one or the other must be destroyed. The whole foreign policy of Russia ever since that time has been based on that theory. It is the answer to Russian tactics in the United Nations and in every committee of which she is a member.
Lenin also stated that when communism is weak is the time to talk peace and ask for peace, but always bearing in mind that communism cannot exist in this world alongside democracy; that when she makes peace or signs any pact of peace, it is only a temporary expedient to be cast aside when the expediency is over. I do not need to remind this house that that is what happened early in the last war when Mr. Molotov was sent to Berlin to sign a non-aggression pact with Germany. He did so because Russia at that time was afraid of Germany. When Poland was divided between Germany and Russia, Russia pushed her frontiers west as far as she could. She did that on the basis of expediency, because Russia has always traded space for time. She did not trust the Germans. She thought that by signing that pact she would at least delay the German attack, and she did.
She went into Poland, and Poland took the first brunt of the German attack. Russia retreated bit by bit, gradually wearing down the Germans. She was fighting for her life. All during that struggle we wanted to help her, and we did. We wanted to send her men in addition to munitions, and she refused. She did not want our men to come in contact with her people, because they would then become acquainted with our way of life, and it would possibly destroy the strength of the Kremlin in so fair as their peoples may have their eyes opened to our way of life.
Before going on I should like to pay a tribute to the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who spoke in this debate two days ago. He gave us a resume of what happened in the United Nations during the last session. If I could sum up what he said I would say his remarks were predicated on one point and one point only, namely, that the success of all the committees which were formed to help the people

External Affairs
in this world and to maintain peace was subject to Russian co-operation. I quote from his speech at page 759 of Hansard as follows:
It is fair to say. I think, that on the whole the recent session of the general assembly neither increased nor decreased the existing tension between the Soviet and the free world. On the other hand, a number of resolutions were approved which, if they can be put into effect, may serve to lessen that tension. In the main, their success will depend upon the desire of the Soviet union to make them work.
These are very serious words. Again he says at page 762:
Here for the first time almost all countries of the free world have co-operated in pooling their resources to give technical assistance to governments which are in need and which request it, but of course the Soviet bloc refused to participate, despite their constant professions of solicitude for the welfare of the peoples of the underdeveloped countries.
We are now living in a state of crisis.
Almost from week to week we have a crisis breaking out in one part of the world or another. I wish to examine, if I may, for a short space of time, the Korean situation. There we have our men, our Canadians, fighting alongside the other allied nations. It will be remembered that some time 'ago, when we were pushing the North Koreans back to the Yalu river, the Chinese came to their assistance and we had to retreat hurriedly back to about where we began, or perhaps a bit farther back. It was hoped then that we could have ended the Korean war on a note of victory. But China came in, and we had to retreat.
General Ridgway was appointed, and he went out there. He evolved a strategy of wearing down the enemy. We attacked and, bit by bit, by our superior gunfire it was said that we were destroying the Chinese army. In the words of the communiques of that time, we were chewing them up; we had them beaten to such an extent that China could not take much more.
What happened? Mr. Malik from the United Nations sounded out the nations on our side in that organization with respect to an armistice. We agreed, because we could not do anything else; and armistice negotiations have been going on in Korea for seven or eight months. There is no sign yet of a real armistice.
Why was that done? If you will remember the few words I spoke a few moments ago you will recall I said that it is the policy of Russia, when she is in difficulty, to sue for peace. The Chinese did not ask for an armistice; it was done through Mr. Malik, the Russian representative in the United Nations. We have in Korea today a situation described as a stalemate. During the

six or seven months the negotiations have been going on the communist forces in Korea have been strengthening their position, so that today we cannot drive them out -or, if so, only with tremendous losses which we cannot afford, and which it would be foolish to risk.
The statement has been made in the house and in the United Nations that our policy in Korea was to unify the whole country. No one can tell me here tonight that we can do that now. That policy enunciated in the United Nations stands as the United Nations policy for Korea. We shall have to back down from that policy sooner or later; and when we do, the United Nations as a policy making machine will get a very black eye, indeed.
I have no brief for General Mac Arthur; but whatever may be said of his military plans in Korea as to how to win the war, this much can be said, that his administration of Japan was brilliant in the extreme; and it has yet to be proven whether his strategy in Korea was wrong or otherwise.
Two years ago I drew attention to the island of Formosa and said that if it fell into communist hands the door would be thrown wide open to the Philippines. It was not a nice thing to say in the house at that time; because our policy was that of trying to keep out of Formosa and its troubles. But it is recognized today that we cannot afford to let Formosa go. And so the United States is taking over as the protector of that island, I
Why did Russia, the communists, attack in Korea? They wanted to gain Korea because it would be a dagger pointed at the heart of Japan. They know that Japan is a warlike nation, and they want Japan within the' communist orbit in the Far East. And I say1 here tonight, without fear of successful contradiction, that it was only the brilliant administration of General MacArthur that kept Japan where it is today.
To go on, now, to Indo-China. When we were chewing up the Chinese armies in Korea there was a lull in Indo-China. China had1 her hands full in Korea and she could not' supply the communist forces. We made headway there. But since these truce negotiations have been going on in Korea they have had time to renew their strength, with the result that we see communist activities breaking out now in Indo-China.
Reports coming from France are that they cannot very well carry on in Indo-China, and . there is a movement afoot for France to 'withdraw from that point. If that happens, then Thailand or Siam will go, and so will Burma, and we shall have then communist

influence right down on the border of the Federated Malay States. Can we then hold the Federated Malay States? I doubt very much if we can. And if we lose the Federated Malay States we lose the rubber and tin we so badly need for rearmament. We shall have communist influence right up to the front door of Indonesia.
Those are problems which are to the forefront today, and I must point them out if we are to have a true picture of the international situation as it now exists. India has her hands full. She and Pakistan are quarrelling over Kashmir. So India cannot be any great help to us. As a matter of fact her actions in the United Nations during the last session or two have indicated a policy of going it alone: she does not wish to get mixed up either with the west or with communism.
Coming to Persia, we have a situation where we have lost the use of its oil. Russia, with diabolical cleverness, has been urging the Persians to stand on their own feet and, with a cry of "Persia for Persians", we are denied the use of their oil. I do not think many members in the house realize just how serious that loss is to us, or how serious it will be if we ever get into a shooting war.
Then the crisis in Persia was followed by the crisis in Cairo. That has died down somewhat. Now we have a crisis in Tunisia. Where is it all going to end? We have adopted here a policy of peace through strength. That policy was adopted1 by all parties in the house. We need strength today as we never needed it before. The men who represent us at the United Nations must be strong. Those who represent us in the countries I have just mentioned must be strong, and we must back their strength. Any sign of weakness will be fatal now, and we may well lose any fight in which we engage.
All the attacks by Russia are directed to one source. Russia realizes where the strength of the United Nations stands. She realizes full well that there is one nation that stands for democracy, so that all her attacks today are directed' against the United States of America. Russia knows that if the United States weakens, then democracy throughout the whole world will weaken.
The United States has never wished world leadership; it was forced upon hbr. What that country does today may mean either peace or war in this world. Because of this position, we cannot afford to have the United States falter. We are bound to the United States hand and foot, not only for the defence of the North American continent, but for the defence of peace in the world.
External Affairs
Let us not here in this House of Commons snipe at the United States for what they are doing. We are not helping the cause of peace when we snipe at them; we are weakening it. Whether we agree or disagree with the United States policy, if we cannot applaud them then let us keep quiet. If we do not back the United States today, we lose; and if the United States goes down, we go down with it.
I am concerned over the spirit of petty nationalism growing up in this country. It is all very well here in the House of Commons to stick out your chest and say "We want Canada for Canadians." I am a new Canadian; but I came into this union, not for any petty benefits that may accrue to my province. We came into the union because we had vision as to what the union could do. And our coming in has strengthened Canada. We knew it would strengthen Canada; and by strengthening Canada we strengthen ourselves.
I am not asking here tonight for union between the United States and Canada; but I am asking for full co-operation with the United States, because in union there is strength. We must demonstrate that strength by a union of ideas and, backing up our thoughts with our actions, we must not give only lip service to union, but must live it. We in Canada must lift up our eyes. We must have world vision. Canada cannot live to itself alone. To adopt a policy of isolationism for this country would be to commit national suicide. I should like to quote from a dispatch which appeared in today's Ottawa Citizen quoting General Charles de Gaulle. While General de Gaulle is not a great favourite of mine, I think there is much food for thought in what he said. The article reads:
General Charles DeGaulle told a group of United States editors Wednesday that the west should act as if a Soviet attack was an immediate danger.
"Then if it happens, the west will be better prepared," said DeGaulle. "If it doesn't happen, then the Lord be praised."
When one of the party asked if the General expected a Russian attack in the near future, DeGaulle replied:
"I do not want, and I cannot make any predictions, but we must act as if this were an immediate threat."
He added that "the present situation cannot last for ever. We must oblige the Russians to renounce their plans for aggression."
DeGaulle criticized the North Atlantic Treaty Organization as being based on an overly narrow concept of defence.
"The danger is a world danger," he said, "and it must be met on a world scale, not merely in the North Atlantic. It should be organized by the three great western powers-the United States, Britain and France-in co-operation with Germany in Europe and with Japan in the Far East."

External Affairs
In my view co-operation or unity or whatever you have a mind to call it is vitally necessary in this world today if we are to defeat communism and therefore we should all be persuaded of the need for each and every one of us, not only talking union but living union. In that way we shall be doing our duty and we as Canadians will be taking our places alongside the peoples of other great nations who are fighting this battle for peace. Upon what we do here and how we do it may very well depend the peace of the world.
It is our duty as Canadians from the east to the west, whatever our racial origin may be, to make unity in Canada a living reality and thereby demonstrate our strength and that we are in this fight for peace and mean to see it through.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all may I congratulate the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) upon delivering a speech which has in it the ring of reality and which has given an indication of the fact that we are discussing no academic problem, that we are talking about survival itself. In the remarks which he has made he has brought to this chamber an atmosphere of reality-
And patriotism.

External Affairs
briefly, and that is the implication of the words the minister used concerning the island of Formosa. He used words which, in that particular case, are not open to doubt.
Would the leopards who sneaked out behind the curtains kindly talk less loudly?
I do not know to whom the hon. member is referring.
The noise, sir, is such that I do not know whether we are hearing about Formosa or Shanghai.
If there is any noise behind the curtains, all I can do is ask for co-operation of the whips to have it reduced.

In the remarks relating to the island of Formosa, the Secretary of State for External Affairs made it clear that he did not believe, and therefore that the government did not believe, that any consideration should be given to the possibility of handing over the island of Formosa to China under its communist government, while there is continuing aggression in Asia by that government. There would have been no occasion to draw that distinction unless the minister had intended us to understand that, if the open acts of aggression of which China is so manifestly guilty at this moment were, in fact, terminated by some agreement emerging from the present negotiations in Korea, then this government would be ready to consider the possibility of handing over the island of Formosa to the control of the communist government of China. The minister goes farther, and he says he does not believe that the presence of a communist regime in China is any reason, in itself, why Formosa should not be handed over if that should be the conclusion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is not a subject that has anything to do with the support of Chiang Kai-shek or any other individual. This subject relates to millions of human beings living on the island of Formosa; it relates to eight million human beings who were living there before Chiang Kai-shek went to the island of Formosa. This implied suggestion that the Canadian government might be quite ready to be party to an arrangement under which the island of Formosa would be handed over, with its population, to the communist government in China lays down a principle which could have the most evil and dangerous consequences if it should ever be accepted by this or any other government in the western world. In those bloody years following the terrible decision at Munich how often was it repeated that never in the future would the word "appeasement" be written in letters of
(Mr. Drew.)
blood across the face of the world! Yet in what way would the handing over of Formosa differ from the handing over of the Sudetenland to the nazi government in Berlin following those discussions in Munich? The principle is the same, namely, that of dealing with millions of human beings as though they were pawns in a game of diplomacy where the cards are being dealt under the table.
There are those in this chamber and a great many outside of it whose memories go back to the high hopes with which everyone greeted, on November 11, 1918, the armistice which ended what had till then been the most terrible war in all history. It will be remembered that in the discussions which followed that armistice and preceded the gatherings at Versailles where there took place the discussions which resulted in the formulating of the treaty of peace and the drafting of the covenant of the league of nations, one of the great leaders of that time, Woodrow Wilson, over and over again emphasized the fact that if peace was to be preserved in the future the days of secret diplomacy must end and that nations must deal with each other on the basis of agreements openly discussed and openly reached with the knowledge of the people who would be affected by those agreements.
We want no secret agreements with regard to Formosa or any other country in the world. If we mean what we said in the charter of the United Nations, at San Francisco in the spring of 1945, the honour of every one of us is pledged to insist that there shall be no secret deals which hand human beings over to the cruel mastery of any dictatorship, such as those which have passed into the sorry pages of history or such as that which now, from Moscow, enslaves so many hundreds of millions of people. We want to be assured that in the course we follow we shall know what that course really is. If once again young Canadians or the youth of any other democracy with which we are now associated are to be called upon to bear arms in the defence of freedom, at least let us be able to tell them that they were not led to slaughter because of sordid trades which dealt with human lives as though they were only pawns in international arrangements of this kind.
To those eight million people living in Formosa freedom is just as dear as it is to us; and make no mistake about it, that freedom from the domination of Peking means the hope of avoiding a dreadful reality which we have not yet been called upon to contemplate here in Canada.
I speak of secret arrangements, and I do so for a particular reason. All the members of

this house will recall the emphasis that was placed by the government of Canada upon the advantage of the close association between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom last year. The members of this house will recall the assurance which was given that the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom were dealing with these problems on the basis of complete confidence and complete understanding. There was, in fact, more than the suggestion that it was extremely fortunate that the government of the United Kingdom, with our knowledge, had restrained the United States from commitments which might have carried hostilities beyond the mainland of Korea. That being so, there is an explanation due to this house. Was the Canadian government aware of the arrangement between Mr. Attlee and Mr. Morrison on the one hand, and the government of the United States on the other, and of the possible extension of hostilities to the bases on the China coast in the event of pressure which would justify that action under the arrangement which was arrived at?
When that arrangement was disclosed in the House of Commons at Westminster a short time ago, it was the disclosure of an arrangement which greatly shocked the people of Britain, not so much because of the arrangement itself as because of the fact that it was an arrangement which had been made without the knowledge of the House of Commons and without the knowledge of the people of Great Britain. Either the Canadian government knew of that arrangement or it did not. If it knew of that arrangement, then we in the house should have known of that arrangement in complete detail. If it did not know of that arrangement, then there was not, between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada, that measure of confidence which we had a right to expect. Whichever it was, the disclosure of that fact should persuade every member of this house that if there is one thing above all others which we will insist upon, as members of the Canadian House of Commons, it is that we know every essential fact upon which the future action of this country might be based.
It is not enough for the government to say: we have the responsibility for policy and at some time, at our convenience, this policy will be placed before the House of Commons and the House of Commons can express its opinion. In this world of rapidly moving events which could so profoundly affect the lives of every one of us for years and scores of years to come, we should not at any time face the possibility that we may discover

The hon. member is at liberty to quote the Toronto Star on any occasion he sees fit. I am quoting a very reliable publication known as the London Times. The editorial is headed: "The Phantom Army", and I quote:
It is difficult to understand either the meaning or the purpose of the communique published by the council of the North Atlantic treaty in Lisbon. This states in words which seem almost to have been chosen for their ambiguity-they have no other virtue-that the member nations will provide this year "approximately fifty divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness." Only the most ingenuous will suppose that General Eisenhower will in fact have fifty divisions ready and able to fight in Europe by the end of the year. The exact figures are rightly secret, but the present force is generally believed to be much less than half that number. Since no German divisions will be raised this year, since contributions from Greece and Turkey are not included in this total, and since France has been allowed to reduce her contribution from fourteen to twelve, it is not easy to see how this figure can be substantially increased. Certainly Britain is not going to send more divisions to Europe this year, and it would be surprising indeed if the United States were to fill the gap. The explanation probably is that the phrase "in appropriate conditions of combat readiness" is meant to include not only divisions fully trained and equipped for war but other divisions half-trained and half-equipped, reserve divisions like our own territorial units, and yet other divisions which so far exist only on paper. No doubt it is necessary to plan for such an expansion, but it is less obvious why it should be announced in this airy fashion.
Presumably the announcement was meant to impress someone; but it will not impress the Russians, who know very well the true state of affairs and who have the sense to realize that any real plans for real divisions would be kept secret. Indeed this imaginative total, with the still more imaginative promise of 85 or 100 divisions in two years time, seems to contain the maximum amount of provocation with the minimum amount of deterrent effect.
That is as far as I propose to quote from the editorial, which goes on at some length to indicate the nature of the statement.

But it does point out that the trouble was that there was apparently a desire to combine security with political propaganda.
Now political propaganda at this stage is' not good enough. And this statement, remember, is a statement for which the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as chairman of the council, accepts responsibility. I believe an explanation is due members of the house and due other nations of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, through this house, as to exactly what the circumstances were under which that strange document became public, and why it was that this phantom army was paraded before the world to lure into a false sense of security our own people, and to irritate the Russians, who know perfectly well it is not accurate, and who certainly will repeat to their own people the fact that this is a declaration that the North Atlantic treaty nations are greatly expanding their forces for the possibility of aggression.
We know it is not aggression. We know that not only would we not contemplate aggression, but that we are utterly incapable of aggression. We know perfectly well that it is beyond the thought of anyone living in Canada, the United States, Great Britain, France or any other of the member nations of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization even to dream of aggression. But what every one of us is hoping for, and what every one of us is prepared to support, and what everyone wants done is the preparation of real divisions, real defence, so that there may be no war, so that peace may be more than a hope, and so that we may march forward in security to a time when even those nations now beyond the iron curtain may join us in the freedom we wish to preserve in this world.
It will not be done however either by misleading our own people or by issuing to Russia challenging statements which are not supported by the facts.

The party I lead has no intention of supporting any proposition, direct or implied, that the preparation now taking place is too much. The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated his hope, in the speech he made, that before this debate was closed it would be clear that the members of this house are one in their determination that Canada shall take its full part in those collective measures designed to prevent war and to preserve peace.
I wish no doubt to be left in the mind of any hon. member or of any Canadian that members of the Conservative party in this house subscribe to that principle without reservation. We have indicated our position; we certainly withdraw in no way from that position. Our concern is that we shall take our full part along lines that will make the most effective use of whatever resources of this country are committed to that collective purpose by the government of Canada.
In saying that we want more information, I am saying so in the hope that before this debate is closed the foundation will be laid for a discussion of national defence, with knowledge of those commitments to which the preparation for national defence is

related. I do not subscribe to the interpretation of some of the statements made by the leader of the C.C.F. party, and others, which was placed upon those statements by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; but I do simply wish to indicate that already in this house I have made it clear that we do not agree with their statement, that we think it was an unfortunate statement, and moreover that it was a statement which is inconsistent with the obligations we have undertaken and which were unanimously supported by members of the house.
I wish to point out also that I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) inadvertently drew a meaning from the editorials in the London Times, the Economist, and the Spectator which those editorials do not contain. The editorials were not critical of the targets; they were critical of the statement that those targets were going to be reached before it was possible for them to be reached.
Nowhere in the editorial in the London Times, nowhere in the editorial in the Economist and nowhere in any of the other editorials along similar lines have I seen any suggestion that the targets were too high. But what this editorial in the London Times, to which I have referred, says, is that the statement issued from Lisbon was unwise and improper because it gave the impression that these targets were going to be reached sooner than they could be reached, and that on the one hand they misled our own people and lured them into a false sense of security while, on the other, it could only be provocative to the Russians, without in any way misleading them as to what the facts actually are.
No; I wish to make it abundantly clear that I regret, as I am sure all members of the Conservative party in the house regret, that there should be an amendment before us at this time which could be interpreted outside of Canada as a suggestion that the House of Commons is not wholly united behind a policy of collective action to prevent war and to maintain peace by the strength of the nations of the Atlantic community, combined in the most effective way that can be done. Nevertheless we certainly do not challenge the right or the propriety of any such amendment. I simply wish to make it clear that we shall not vote for that amendment, that we do assert our support of the principles which have been enunciated, and that we return to the statement regarding the principles of NATO which met with approval when they were enunciated in this house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

In so far as we adhere to the principle of collective action to prevent war, I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs will at all times receive the support of every member of the Conservative party sitting in this House of Commons. It is because we want to see that principle implemented in terms of reality that we are asking now that he take this house into his confidence and tell us what the facts really are, that he remove the uncertainty to which great publications like the London Times, the Economist and others in our own country have referred in words that leave no doubt about the confusion which now exists.
If we are going to be called upon to vote billions of dollars to be provided by the taxpayers of Canada let us be able to tell the taxpayers of Canada what those dollars are being spent for. Above all, let us not be in the position where it can be said that anything that is done in this house is justification for the proposition that diplomacy is the mother of deception. If we are going to respect the diplomacy by which we are represented in the councils of the world, if we are going to respect the diplomacy of the nations which are joined in this great undertaking to prevent war, let us put an end to secret under-the-table deals. Let us have the facts out in the open. On that basis this house and the people of Canada will stand behind the government if it really carries out the undertakings that it makes.

Mr. Speaker, most of the speeches during this debate have centred on the work done at the last meeting of the United Nations in Paris and the report made by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization which met in Lisbon, as well as on the situation in the Far East and assistance to underdeveloped countries. The government's position on these questions has been expressed clearly by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and his parliamentary assistant, and I shall make only a few references to some of the statements made by members on these questions before I deal with other aspects of the international situation.
Before I took the floor the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) addressed the house.
I must confess that each time the gentleman gets up I take great pleasure in listening.
I admire his wonderful voice, his imposing bearing. My pleasure would be nearly perfect if the ideas which his words are intended to impart were as great, as judicious and as weighty as the voice that expresses them is nice and deep and melodious.

The first part of the hon. gentleman's remarks dealt with a statement previously made that new policies had been announced by the minister of external affairs outside this house. I quite agree that that would not be proper because previously I criticized another member of the cabinet for doing that. I think the answer to this part of the hon. gentleman's speech can be found on page 662 of Hansard of March 21, and therefore I do not have to deal with it further.
The second part of his speech dealt with the statement issued by the department of publicity of NATO after the Lisbon meeting.
I imagine that that statement had been weighed and considered by the proper responsible officials and represented the views and thoughts of the leaders of that organization.
I think everybody in Canada will understand that that was a statement for NATO, of NATO, the responsibility for which rests with the chairman of NATO. I think the statement can be defended in itself. I think the statement is good and that the minister of external affairs will be able to make it stand on its own feet. As far as we in this house are concerned, I think the way we should deal with it is to just realize that at that time the minister was acting in his capacity- a higher capacity because it concerns a supranational organization-as head of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and not in his capacity as a member of the Canadian government. I am sure that when he winds up the debate the minister will be able to speak for himself and I have no brief to defend him at this time.
Criticism has been voiced in certain quarters as to the so-called insufficient part taken by Canada in helping the economy of other nations who are members of NATO. We have been told that the United States are doing much more than we could do, and that we should emulate them. I am all in agreement with those who want to provide economic aid in order to prevent the spread of communism among European nations, but I do suggest that the problem must be tackled realistically, having in mind not only our mutual security but above all our own security and our own welfare. Our first duty is to Canada and to Canadians.
No matter how much we want to implement article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty, which is the article dealing with the understanding among the members to help one another, to eliminate conflicts in international economic policies and so on, we must realize the far greater importance of defending one another against possible threat from other nations or 55704-56

groups of nations who may want to impose their imperialistic domination or their ideology of government on the western world.
Canada's share in the NATO economic program should be commensurate with our ability to pay, with our income and with our population. I would not for one minute suggest that we should not assume our full share of the joint preparedness to resist attack; I would not suggest that we should not help less fortunate nations. But I do object to our overburdening our people, as we would have to do were we to carry out all the suggestions made by hon. members. Among those suggestions is the suggestion that we should make available free of charge to other member nations of NATO certain raw materials and basic commodities. The fact is that the sale of those articles ensures our own economic balance and guarantees the welfare of our own people.
We have entered, and rightly so, an era of mutual help among nations. We are opposing Russian communism as well as Chinese communistic dictatorship. But that does not mean that we should endanger unduly our own program of social security at home. There is a limit beyond which we cannot go without threatening our national economy. I think on the whole Canada's program has been realistic and well balanced. Year after year we have voted more and more funds to ensure a minimum of social security to our own people. Not only have I approved of all of this; I would like to see it expanded. I have oftentimes said that aid should be provided for invalids, as well as a system of health insurance for those whose health is impaired.
For the three years starting in 1950 our defence program, whether at home or for the fulfilment of our obligations abroad, first in Korea and now in the European sphere of activity, will involve an expenditure of over $5,000 million. Even if the potential of our country is extremely vast, would it be right to increase our commitments without due regard to our ability at this time to pay both for our own program of social security and for defence here and abroad?
Furthermore, we should not minimize what we have already given in the way of assistance to other NATO countries. In the last years this has amounted to $320 million, which is of course exclusive of the $25 [DOT] 4 million voted for the Colombo plan and our own share of $3-2 million of the cost of administration of NATO. There may be other amounts which I have not been able to ascertain, and no doubt the minister will give them when he closes the debate.

One member has suggested that we should expand our food production and give it away to member nations of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. That would be along the lines of what we did when we gave Great Britam $3,000 million during the war, and it would all have to be paid by the Canadian taxpayer. I wonder how much the carrying out of this and other suggestions would mean in taxes over the years to come and in an increase in the national debt which would have to be looked after by coming generations.
Apart from the United States, which is the most powerful and wealthiest of our allies; apart from the great empires of yesterday, the United Kingdom and France, who are still vastly wealthier than we are, Canada is the one nation of the world who has spent more in a most unselfish way, both during the last war and the present world crisis that is also called the cold war, than any other nation. I would even say she is spending more than many other wealthier nations on this hemisphere to build up the joint defences of the western democracies, and to help the less fortunate countries.
I think that we all agree that what we have done is sound policy, even if our share has been greater than that of many. But I do not like to see what we have done minimized, as has been done in different quarters in this house. 1 doubt if it would be in the interests of our country or our allies to endanger our own economic position in the hope of giving more encouragement to others, as has been urged. In considering our commitments for defence or economic aid, one must take a proper outlook and consider, not only the day to day incidents that affect the international situation, but the over-all picture. This global struggle is totally different from anything history has so far revealed. This so-called cold war may last longer than some may think. It may well be that soviet strategy is to act in such a way as to make this unhealthy state of affairs last interminably.
I have here a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of July 26, 1951, and it confirms what I have just said about the possible length of this cold war. It reads:
. . . the western world . . . may suddenly realize that it has been fighting world war III for years and never knew it.
Certainly any such recognition has seemed far away from most public statements by most public figures. For them another world war has been a dim, far-off event, the date of which (for reasons never entirely clear), is generally about seven years away. As for the struggle now taking place, that is never THE war. It is always a struggle that will be contained. The assurance is given that there are no imminent signs that Russia intends to launch another world war.

But this struggle in Korea, whatever it may be called, suggests that even if Russia never launches a massive world war of the old, orthodox Germanic type, it may still fight a war around the world of a new unorthodox type. And if Russia develops a new type of world war, it may be able to outflank all the preparations that the west has been making for a war that may never be fought.
The article goes on:
Indeed Russia, while fighting its new type of world war III, can exploit to the limit the west's anxiety not to open a world war of the massive and universal type. Russia can be exceedingly provocative, as it certainly was in Korea. But it will count upon the west immediately saying that there is every hope that this war will not spread into a general conflict.
In this way Russia can go on fighting around the world, using open field aggression at one point, as in Korea: using tenacious guerrilla fighting in another, as in Burma and in Malaya; using infiltration and incitement in another, as in Iran; dangling appeals to nationalist unity in yet another, as in Germany; . . .
By fighting world war III in this tenacious but piecemeal manner, Russia could force the west to fight on Russia's terms, while the west prepares for a type of war that Russia may never invite and which the west would be most reluctant ever to launch. The west may be manoeuvred into fighting Russia's kind of world war III, while saying all the while that it is not a world war at all.
For Russia nothing could be better. While the west stockpiles the weapons of mass destruction, Russia could pursue its technique of mass exhaustion.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while we must do our part by helping to prevent other nations from falling prey to communism wherever we can, I suggest we would be remiss in our duty if we failed to keep conditions in our own country such that our population will continue to enjoy the present standard of living. That is the best guarantee that our own people will feel contented with their present form of government, and their present way of life.
Before I conclude the first part of my remarks, I should like to point out that Canada is the only country of which I know where the opposition parties complain that the government has not sufficiently burdened the country with international commitments, our obligations to NATO or other international bodies. Everywhere else, including the United States, opposition parties have tried to cut down their countries' commitments. Even in Great Britain, the left wing of the Labour party tries to cut that country's expenditures earmarked for defence. When one reads the reports by British, French and United States foreign correspondents, one sees that the trend in most countries is to criticize the commitments for economic aid or for defence purposes as too high, and not to minimize them as we have witnessed here. We can, therefore, conclude that the Canadian government's program, as I said earlier, is well balanced and sufficiently generous at the moment. If

the people of Canada do not want, as I said a moment earlier, to be overburdened with taxes in the years to come or even today, how much more could we do than is provided for in the government's program?
During the course of this debate we have heard an hon. member state what, fortunately, only a small group of people in my province are saying. I feel it my responsibility, however, to mention it, so that such false and dangerous reasoning may not spread. The tenet of this thesis is that prayers may assure peace, and that preparedness for defence is the sure way to war. The hon. member said "Peace must be deserved and earned by our prayers". I would be the last one to deny anyone the right to pray for peace. I would be the last one to discourage a person from doing so. But I say that anybody who would meet the modern weapons or the powerful armies of those who threaten the peace of the world merely by prayers would not be allowed to pray very long if they survived the onslaught or if ever Soviet Russia ruled the world.
I quite agree with the hon. member when he states that if the leaders of the nations of the world, "instead of sowing the seeds of discord, hatred and revenge through their speeches and the newspapers in their pay, would put into practice God's supreme command, 'Love thy neighbour', there would be more peace and happiness on earth and the din of war would subside." But this noble attitude would have to be two-sided to have any effect, and in the present state of the world we have very little evidence that the other side intends to behave so nobly. If a peaceful citizen, Mr. Speaker, goes along a street and is suddenly faced by a big bully who jumps on him and tries to knock him down, even if he kneels down to pray I think he will just offer a better angle to the man who wants to strike him. If that fellow expected he might meet that big bully at that corner, I think what he ought to do would be to get a few friends to join him in his walk, so that seeing many ready to support one another the big bully would not dare to attack them. That is what we are doing with NATO. We are ganging together to prevent a big bully from jumping on us when we do not want him to do so. The NATO countries are combining their strength and force in order to resist jointly rather than be knocked down separately.
At school we all learned the famous maxim "si vis pacem, para bellum." I think it is still eminently practical as long as we translate it, "if you want peace to be maintained, make sure your defences are adequate."
