I think it is also misleading for that hon. member to say that "we have forfeited a part of our sovereignty in favour of a supranational sovereignty which is subject to the whim of circumstances and to the dictates of the financial leaders interested in their gold mining enterprise or their munitions plants, and we are fostering internationalism at the expense of patriotism." This is not only misleading; it is false. It is a most dangerous theory to propagate and when my hon. friend, to substantiate another of his arguments, quotes' Pierre Cot, a former French minister of whom the least we can say is that be is a fellow traveller, he plays the game of the very people whom I am convinced he must of necessity abhor.
The United Nations is far from being perfect, we all agree. I would not be one to say that the fault is all on one side. However, any student of world affairs who has at heart our democratic way of life and our institutions will recognize that the stumbling block to demobilization and the bringing about of peaceful conditions in the world has been Soviet Russia and her satellites. However imperfectly the United Nations may work, it constitutes the only point of contact we can maintain with the U.S.S.R. I think it is preferable for all concerned to meet these, people at the conference table rather than in a shooting war that would give a stunning blow to humanity, whoever may emerge as the victor.
My hon. friend should know, I think, that no western leader wants war. I am quite sure he would also recognize that the leaders of the Canadian government-in fact I shall gladly say the leaders of all parties in this house-do not want war. But he should also recognize that they would fail in their duty if they did not meet the situation that faces the world and our country today with appropriate measures to ensure our defence and the mutual security of the western world on which our own security greatly depends. When one ponders over the international situation at large, many other and most important considerations force themselves upon, us. What are the chances of avoiding an armed conflict at the present time is evidently the foremost. According to me, neither the United States and the western democracies- or call them the North Atlantic treaty nations, if you which-nor Russia and its satellites wish a shooting war or intend to start one voluntarily, but this state of mind is not enough to guarantee that we shall not have one.
In 1914 Germany might not have precipitated a war had it been convinced that Britain and the commonwealth would enter

External Affairs
the war and it would certainly have waited had it foreseen American intervention. In 1939 Hitler might not have gone ahead had the United States taken the stand they took in 1941, and had Hitler been convinced that eventually he would have to face at the same time the combined forces of the United States, the U.S.S.R., joined to the British commonwealth, the war might have been averted. This is the reasoning that is today at the basis of the determined joint action of the North Atlantic treaty nations and of all other united nations which might join them if war started. This is our best assurance that we may avoid a conflict. However, no matter how improbable it is that any of the two blocs might start a war voluntarily, the danger persists that they may be drawn into one by any move undertaken at a given point on the globe. The risk arises in a way from the indetermination of the zones of influence considered important by the opponents and the undefined interest one side may have to prevent a given area from falling within the field of action of the other. Such was the case in Korea. It is evidently to be deplored that the lives of Canadians, Americans and citizens of other United Nations countries should be risked or even sacrificed in that fight. But it is recognized that had not the United States and the United Nations taken the stand they did there would have been no limit to the expansion of Soviet domination in the Orient.
In Europe the situation is more clearly defined and the determination of the western democracies, synthetized by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and by the Council of Europe, is manifested in such a way as to leave no doubt as to what action on the part of the Soviet may precipitate war. There remains the question of Yugoslavia that poses a grave problem. Some countries might hesitate to risk war to prevent one powerful communist country from overruling a smaller communist country impoverished by the last war and largely undeveloped by its previous so-called democratic rulers. Yet during the last war we did not hesitate to ally ourselves with the U.S.S.R. in order to defeat nazism and fascism. I personally think that our own interest today lies in preventing the domination of Yugoslavia by Russia. Once that domination was effected, the supremacy of the Mediterranean would no longer be ours and Turkey and Greece, who are, in the first case an already powerful ally and in the second, a most important bastion of defence, would both be in danger, not to say sacrificed. Anybody who has been in touch with Yugoslav leaders or with Yugoslav officials in their own country, as I have been, comes back convinced that even if these people

are not pro-American and if they are still profoundly Marxist, they are even more antiRussian; that they are determinedly nationalist and know that their survival as an independent nation depends on their co-operation with the western democracies. It should not take any of us very long to consider the factors involved and to understand that it is in our own interest to prevent their country from being overrun by the soviets.
Once all spheres of danger have been the object of precise determination, there remains one important factor that we cannot overlook. For the Russians, the allied determination may constitute a temptation to strike more quickly in the hope of winning. They know their present military superiority and they might hope that if this short-term superiority might compensate for their lower industrial strength, they might win. Yet such reasoning was the undoing of Hitler, and the Politburo does not usually act on the advice of astrologers or crystal gazers. If their knowledge of the long-term superiority of the western nations outbalances their immediate military strength, war may be indefinitely postponed.
Their last move, Mr. Speaker, was their new approach to the question of German unity, which brings me to the last point of my remarks, namely, the dilemma that has faced American, British and French statesmen in the last four years: how to deal with Germany. This, more than any committee work at the United Nations, might be the decisive factor determining the fate of Europe in the years to come, and one of the most important elements in the over-all international situation.
The allied determination to help arm Germany as part of the whole European defence has been the most vivid topic of speculation, especially in Germany and in France, as I gathered during a stay in both countries this last fall. There is no denying that the French have not ceased fearing the possibility of a resurgence of German superiority in Europe and it is quite easy to understand this fear. Harold Callender, chief of the New York Times Paris bureau, in his paper recently gave us a good analysis of the French reaction to the American and British attitude concerning the rearmament of Germany. I recommend its reading to all hon. members since I can, unfortunately, give only one or two quotations. He says of the French:
They are worried by the prospect of the rearming of Germans and of the western world. They are also worried by the economic burden placed upon their convalescent economy by their war in Indochina and their commitments for defence in Europe.

Later in the article he says:
If Americans sometimes feel baffled by the double task of maintaining peace and economic stability, they may imagine the far greater sense of frustration that the French feel when facing similar tasks while lacking both the favourable geographical position and the incomparable resources and power of the United States.
And later:
It was the assurance of the United States support that led the French to take the lead in trying to unite western Europe economically and politically. It was the sudden insistence of the United States upon rearming German units that dismayed the French and led to a hasty compromise between what the French thought were incompatible American policies-a desire to unite Europe and a simultaneous desire to risk alienating France by recruiting a German force . . .
Thus the French are asked to become the cornerstone of a stronger western Europe while at the same time being the cornerstone of the defence of southeast Asia. They say officially though reluctantly that they will try to fill both roles if sufficient United States aid is available.
It was while the French were wondering how they could meet these two heavy tasks that the German question became suddenly acute, first when the United States proposed to rearm the Germans and recently when the Germans boldly stated their stiff price for agreeing to rearm. This brought all the latent French fear of Germany to the surface . . .
It is the fear of both the military power they might acquire, as the French see it, as the result of United States impatience to build up European defences, and of the economic and political power that might come from the new freedom and sovereignty to be accorded to the west German state...
In these circumstances it is perhaps natural for the French to fear that the United States, thinking mainly of defence, might prefer Germany to France as the cornerstone of western Europe. Some Frenchmen recall that once before, at the end of the first world war, the west granted the Germans a limited army from which militarism again grew.
The allied determination to help Germany has created such a problem that all the statesmen of western Europe are pondering over this question and devising, day after day, new ways of approach that may lead to a favourable solution of this problem. Drew Middleton, chief of the New York Times bureau in Germany, also has some interesting comments which I should like to quote. He says:
The United States is chiefly responsible and can claim a major share of the credit for the revival of Germany, if, on the account books of history, credit is due. It is also a development that raises serious problems for Europe and ultimately for the United States, problems that must be weighed against the advantages of adding Germany, temporarily at least, to the western allied side.
The most important of these problems centers around the fear and mistrust of Germany that remain in Europe, and to a lesser degree in the British Isles, and the efficacy of the measures already taken by the United States, Britain and France to ensure that Germany does not again become a threat to Europe's security.
Then later on he states:
Yet, despite the intricate apparatus set up to bind Germany to Europe-the Schuman plan, the European defence community and the council of Europe
External Affairs
-grave doubts exist on the subject of Germany's suitability and reliability as a partner.
Such doubts rest, not on any great hostility to the west German government of today, headed by Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, or on the attitude of that government toward European co-operation, but on the reluctance of Europeans to accept either that government or that policy as representing the real Germany. In a few years the world will be dealing with another government and there is no guarantee that this future government will be any more willing to accept the treaties of 1952 than was the nazi government to maintain the Europe constructed between 1918 and 1925.
The attitude of German governments of tomorrow is the question mark, and offers dangerous possibilities. Visitors to Germany come back with the feeling that Adenauer is perfectly honest and sincere in his dealings with the western leaders. Election results show that at this moment a majority of German voters are behind him; but would that majority and support persist after the departure of the occupation forces? This remains to be seen. I think, however, that my other conclusions about Germany may differ from those reached this afternoon by my friend, the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). No matter how correctly the German authorities act, you sense a constant hostility to the occupation and I suppose it is inevitable. It is less evident, I would say, against the British and the French, but it is quite open against the Americans. I will admit, through personal observation in Germany, that the irritations may well be motivated.
One must realize that never has so much been demanded of a private soldier in a foreign land as from the American G.I. in Germany. Diplomacy and courtesy are hardly to be expected from a man ill-prepared for the feeling of almightiness he gets from a privileged position in a former enemy's land. I am glad to see from the reports we have had recently that the feeling towards our Canadian troops seems to be better. Anyway this is so according to our defence information services. I am glad of that. Irritations against more or less irresponsible and juvenile attitudes or behaviour by some elements of the American troops could hardly explain however the opinions of so many Germans who side with Schumacher, only because he rings a more Chauvinistic note than Adenauer, or of so many more who side with the neo-nazi leaders. I, for one, fear that the average German has not yet understood, and that his mentality has little changed from that of the Germans of 1933 who helped bring Hitler to power. I will not enter into details and give also the feeling one brings from a visit to the crematorium and the concentration camp of Dachau, since we must overlook

External Affairs
a lot in a people we must keep on our side in our present need for European defence.
The Russian move, offering to back up German unity and offering to believe in the purification of the Wermacht and the former nazis, offers new and dangerous possibilities. Carl Sulzberger, writing from Paris last week said, and I am not choosing my authority from French-speaking writers, who I might say are more prejudiced because they feel more the immediate danger, but from an American correspondent:
But the west certainly wishes to avoid two obvious potential risks:
(1)	That such a unified, bitter and dynamic land would be enticed into a marriage of convenience with the Soviet bloc, or
(2)	That the Germans, wooed by both power coalitions, would keep bidding up the price for future collaboration until they regain continental ascendancy.
Later on he says:
Nationalists and militarists dream of a new and militant role in which Germany can assume the position of arbiter between east and west.
That in my opinion is what is dangerous and what is to be feared. Finally, analysing the present move on the part of the Russians, Sulzberger says:
For the third time in three decades the Politburo is openly courting Germany. Thirty years ago, at Bapallo, the Bolshevik envoys concluded a series of clandestine negotiations with an alliance with the German republic. Indemnity claims were renounced. Economic agreements were concluded. And secret military compacts permitted the professional Reichswehr to rebuild.
That policy, eleven- years later, boomeranged against Moscow when Hitler came to power and began his new quest for empire which resulted in the second world war.
In 1939, hoping to steer the Fuehrer's ambitions westward, the U.S.S.R. again gambled on a proGerman policy. Foreign ministers Molotov and Ribbentrop concluded what was virtually an alliance and Hitler confidently began a global conflict ending with the destruction of most of European Russia.
When the nazi empire collapsed and Europe's traditional backbone was broken, Moscow appeared content to see the amputation of Germany for an indefinite period. It sought to communize its portion of the occupied Reich, to remilitarize the east, and- block recovery in the west.
We have now this last attempt, and this promise of accepting members of the nazi party and the Wermacht. This is a new bid to bring about German unification in the hope that this country may one day unite with Russia.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say the principal aim of Europe and of the western world must be to unite to remain free even if in the process of doing so we may gather strange bedfellows and unreliable ones but for Europeans it might be harder than for us. They are facing such a situation that if they IMr. Picard.]
want to survive as free and independent peoples they must solve their problems together while all their historical tradition has been to solve them against one another.
Since the dissolution of the Roman empire, the history of Europe has been the history of wars between European states, and the only attempts at unification were intended to bring about the hegemony of one nation over others.
European nations must, to survive, learn to unite in order to stay free, and leadership must come from this side of the Atlantic. This leadership must take into account every factor and it is the duty of the leaders of western democracy to act prudently.
As far as we in this house are concerned we can do nothing less than support the government's decisions which, on the whole and up to now, appear to be wise and moreover inevitable.

Mr. Speaker, for a comparative novice to the traditions and systems of this parliament it is at times difficult to appreciate exactly what a motion or a resolution means or implies. I candidly admit that I am still in the class of a novice, but I believe it is one of the best established principles that an amendment to the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair in order that supply may be voted to Her Majesty is definitely a vote of want of confidence. If that is the case-and it is-I believe that in my short parliamentary career this is the first time that we have had a major vote of want of confidence moved against the Canadian government, based on foreign policy.
I do not know how far back in Canadian history it would be necessary to go before we could find a major test of strength, a major want of confidence resolution, based on external affairs, but we have it today. That means that the boasts which I have been proud to make, and which I think private members from every party in this house have doubtless been proud to make over the past few years, the boasts that whatever may be done elsewhere we in Canada are at least united in our foreign affairs, united in our front to those who would oppose us, can no longer be made.
This amendment has been moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) of the C.C.F. party, I presume because he honestly believes that it represents the feelings of some body of opinion in this country. I am wondering what body of opinion they think is represented by a want of confidence motion at this time, based on external affairs. I suppose it is quite likely that the intention

is to carry out the spirit of the now well-known press release issued by the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation, and dated March 4, 1952, dealing with external affairs, in which these two sentences appear:
The C.C.F. urges that Canada should vigorously oppose the armaments goals set at Lisbon.
A halt must be called, before it is too late, to the control of NATO by the military and by certain American influences which jeopardize the peaceful and defensive objectives which brought the organization into being.
I would like the house to remember for the moment the wording of that second sentence. Assuming that that was the intention of the mover of the resolution, I wonder if he realizes that, whatever else he is doing, he is not expressing by that resolution in this house the unanimous opinion of those across Canada who support the C.C.F. as a party. The statement from which I just quoted was dated March 4.
I hold in my hand the C.C.F. News published in Vancouver. This is the issue of March 5, in which the leading editorial deals with the same subject. In order that I may be perfectly fair and that I may not be accused of picking out of the editorial just those sentences that appeal to me, I shall place on the record, not necessarily with either relish or approval, the whole editorial. I shall quote it; and, if the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) will forgive the plagiarism, I shall be quoting until I indicate that I have reached the end of the passage. I quote:
Progress at Lisbon
The vague communique issued at the conclusion of the NATO conference at Lisbon shows that NATO waxes stronger, though not as speedily as some wish. Apparently, some division of the military burden was agreed upon, subject to ratification by the member countries, and a permanent political organ for collaboration of the member states is to be created.
For the governments represented at Lisbon to agree upon that division was a great achievement and, no doubt, a bitter task. To persuade the parliaments of the member states to implement the Lisbon decisions is another difficult task and already Mr. Faure's delicately poised French government has fallen on this issue.
There is not only the problem of distributing the burden as between countries; there is also the problem of distributing the burden as between classes within member countries.
All the socialist parties of the NATO countries and of western Germany are agreed upon the principle of common rearmament and common defence, but we are pitted against the capitalist parties of those countries on the division of the burden as between classes and on the issue of socialist versus capitalist modes of social and economic development. The socialist parties nevertheless quarrel among themselves on what may be termed national issues. Thus on the question of European and NATO duties and privileges for western Germany, German and French socialists seem irreconcilable.
Nevertheless the small minority of socialists who can find nothing better to do than whine about

External Affairs
American dominance and the threat of revived German nationalism and the like do the cause of socialism a grave disservice, for they sow only confusion. These are grave problems which will not be resolved by whining and sneering.
The socialist parties of the NATO countries must make their peace, either with their capitalist parties or with the Kremlin, and they have elected the former. As socialists, our job is to strengthen the voice of socialism within the councils of the NATO countries and of NATO itself. We must urge a fair distribution of the military burden from a working class point of view and a coming to grips with social and economic problems, the solution of which is vital no less to defence than to all other good considerations.
Meanwhile, let us record, in a mood not of despair but of hope, that there was progress at Lisbon.
That, apparently, is the considered viewpoint of at least some of those who are glad to call themselves C.C.F. supporters in this country; and I am glad to say that it is that section of the C.C.F. which comes from my province.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the next question which occurs to me is this: Being a vote of non-confidence, it is a vote of non-confidence in what? Is it non-confidence in the Canadian government? Well, the fact that it is introduced in this House of Commons would leave that as a fair assumption. Is it not also a vote of non-confidence in NATO itself?
I know the hon. member who offered the amendment made that clear, because at page 769 of Hansard for March 25 he is reported in this way:
The impression seems to have been created in the house and in the country that, because we in this group agree that a position of strength must be attained if peace is to be maintained-or, should I say, if war is not to spread farther-we agree with the present government policy with respect to NATO.
I want to say, and as decidedly as I can, that this is not the case. While we do agree with the overall objective, we certainly disagree with the methods by which this government is presently trying to implement that objective.
It occurs to me that a great many sound newspapermen are going to find it their duty to forward, as a news item of import, to a great many countries vitally concerned, the terms of the hon. member's resolution, a resolution which has news merit. But it also occurs to me that the average newspaperman may decide that it is not necessarily up to him to forward the terms of the hon. member's speech, because apparently that has neither value nor merit.
He has not explained to us in the terms of his resolution just in what way the government could have-and I quote his words- taken "effective steps to achieve the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty", by itself. And so I presume, whether he intended it so or not-and he cannot read

External Affairs
it otherwise-the implied want of confidence must extend also to NATO as an organization.
Of course there is a third possibility, that it is also intended as a vote of non-confidence in the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). Speeches made during this debate would seem to bear out that interpretation. We in this house, then, are being asked to endorse a vote of want of confidence in our Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the man from Canada who has such an outstanding record in the whole western world, whose efforts in connection with such matters as the cease-fire talks in respect of Korea made him the idol of the peace-loving countries of the world, a man who is perhaps just another proof of the truth of the biblical quotation, misquoted in this house earlier today, that a prophet is not without honour save in his own country.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada is the man whom I have heard described as the only known case in modern history of somebody having achieved what was formerly regarded as the impossible, a practical idealism. This is the man whom I have heard described, not only by Canadians but by others, as without exception the soundest man in external affairs living in the world today.
Hear, hear.

I was about to add my personal endorsation to that last statement, but I am glad the house has beat me to it.
What I would like to know is this: What is the intent of the amendment? Is it intended to help or to hinder? And, something further I would like to know, even more important than the intent, is this: What is the likely result of the resolution? Is it likely to help the cause for which we are all seeking a solution-and in this I include the mover of the amendment himself. Is it likely to help or is it likely to hinder?
Is it likely to help the Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada, that man who for months has been carrying on his shoulders a burden much larger than should be borne by the representative of any mere fourteen millions of people? Is it likely to help him to go into his future negotiations, when he has knowledge that there has been a vote of want of confidence in him, in his government and, I say, in NATO, and that that vote has been placed upon the records of this parliament? Is it likely to help any representative of Canada who from now on may go to the NATO council, when a record of a vote of non-confidence of this nature is in the back 
of his mind, to be drawn upon arid referred to by those whose objective it is not to help but to hinder?
I say, and I say with sincere regret, that the hon. member who introduced this resolution has done irreparable and incalculable damage. I would hasten to say, and I say this, too, with equal sincerity, that I believe the damage done is far greater than any he anticipated at the time he took this action. But that damage has been done.
I should like the house now for a moment to imagine something almost unthinkable- that the resolution should carry in the house. I assume that no resolution is placed upon the records of the house without some consideration being given to the possibility of its carrying. Supposing this one does carry. Can you imagine the capital that might be made out of that by those whose business it is, not only to disrupt NATO but to disrupt any other organization or any other action directed toward the salvaging of the peace of the world? Let us carry a resolution like this and how long will it be before newspapers, not only in the satellite countries but in those we might describe for want of a better term as the wobbly countries would be carrying headlines such as this: Disunity in NATO or NATO attacked by founder member?
That sort of thing must be the natural result of carrying a resolution like this. A couple of days later somebody would get hold of the real implication and we would see headlines such as this: NATO denounced as purely militaristic organization. Then of course the next step, following the U.S.S.R. type of logic, and they are not slow to follow it when given the slightest excuse, would be to interpret the passing of this resolution as follows: NATO held by Canada to be organ of aggression.
I submit that that is not any exaggeration of the picture of what would happen if this house were to lose completely its sense of proportion and carry such a resolution. They will say, "Oh, it will not pass." I grant that, and that being so, why bring it up? Why has it been placed upon the records of this house? They will say, "To permit debate." That excuse will not do this time because this debate was under way before this resolution was moved. The leader of the hon. gentleman's party had spoken and taken his seat before this resolution was moved.
However, there can still be some salvaging done by this house of the damage which I believe sincerely has occurred already. This house can, and I am confident it will, defeat this ill-advised, misguided resolution by a vote which should turn out to be something like 225 to 13.
Will you ever get that many Liberals here?
We have not that many Liberals but I am sure that on a question like this we can count on more than Liberal support.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has it occurred to the hon. member that the moving of this resolution, and indeed the passing of it, might actually strengthen the hands of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, both in the government and at NATO, for the things he believes in?

I will answer the hon. member's question this way: Nothing quite as absurd as that has occurred to me yet. As I was saying when I was so pleasantly interrupted, this house at least can show the world where the elected representatives of the people of Canada stand. I assure you that if this house defeats that resolution by such an overwhelming figure as the one I quoted it would still be considerably smaller proportionately than the defeat which that same resolution would receive if it were submitted in some form of referendum to the people of Canada. Under those circumstances it would be defeated also by a large number of C.C.F. voters who, to quote their own phraseology, would be only too glad to record, in a mood not of despair but of hope, that there had been progress made at Lisbon.

Mr. Speaker, in the course of this debate, I have listened with great interest to the various speeches which have been made in connection with external affairs. The international situation is very complicated at present and shows the growing imperialistic tendencies of Soviet Russia.
Since the last world cataclysm that Russian bear has constantly been biting at the brave little democracies around it. At the crack of the knout it has silenced the governments of these free peoples behind the iron curtain. Every day brings us the knowledge of some new treachery perpetrated behind that thick curtain. Yesterday, it was Czechoslovakia's turn to be given a new system of government which, far from having been chosen by her, was imposed upon her. In that former free country there were many isolated groups of resistance, but President Benes was soon forced to make a declaration and the suicide of Jan Masaryk followed.
One after another Yugoslavia, Hungary, Bulgaria and Roumania fell, while in each country a strange comedy was played, to mention only the mock trials of Mindszenty, Beran and others. Greece had its own guerrillas. Its borders were violated and shots
External Affairs
fired, and each time satellites of Moscow helped the invader. Immediately after the rape of the Balkans, China was artfully invaded. Chiang Kai-shek went into exile and set up his headquarters on the island of Formosa. North Korea was invaded and the 38th parallel crossed. The United Nations forces met the invader and since then the Korean war has been on, with its shifting from one side of the 38th parallel to the other and its constant danger of being the spark which will start a third world war.
However, the United Nations action testified to the determination of the free peoples of the world to put a stop to the schemings of the soviet aggressor. Shortly before there was born, under the auspices of Benelux, an organization for the federation of western Europe. Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed a treaty of mutual defence and aid in case of aggression. Then France and the United Kingdom joined this organization whose objective was the pursuit of peace. Later, the free nations, conscious of their responsibilities and anxious to safeguard their liberty and to extend a helping hand to the countries which had just lost theirs, signed the North Atlantic treaty.
On the list of the historical documents which are worth mentioning here is one which ranks first both by its objectives and by its comforting effect with regard to the tense international situation.
Here is a monument of international law which for generations will bear witness to the desire of the people of the North Atlantic area to ensure peace in the world and to their determination to take adequate means to that effect. But above all it might make the eager conquerors pause before undertaking their great adventure.
In these times of instability, of uncertainty and of confusion, through the cycles of a cold war or, better, of a war of nerves, the signatories of the treaty have proved their faith in the objects and principles of the charter of the United Nations, their intention to respect human rights and fundamental freedoms, thus ensuring peace in the world and to this end in accordance with the preamble to the charter, to unite their combined efforts in preserving their security.
Every clause of the treaty provides for the adoption of measures which would enable the nations to reach that noble goal. Thus, in accordance with section 1, the parties undertake, as provided in the charter of the United Nations, to settle international disagreements by peaceful means and to refrain from using threats or force in a way which would defeat the aims of the United Nations.

External Affairs
Section 2 of the said treaty bears witness to the fact that these people eagerly wish to develop international, peaceful and friendly relationships by strengthening their free institutions. It provides as well for the development of the conditions which are bound to ensure stability, well-being and economic co-operation between all these nations. The next section deals with mutual assistance and the increasing of the individual and combined capacities of these peoples to resist an armed attack. While section 4 provides for consultation every time it is felt that the territorial integrity of political independence or security of one of these parties is threatened, section 5 recognizes that an armed attack against one or more of these parties in Europe or in North America will be considered as an attack, and that in the case of such an attack the parties will, in accordance with the terms of section 51 of the charter of the United Nations, immediately take, individually or with other parties, such action as is deemed' necessary, including the use of armed strength, to maintain or restore peace in the North Atlantic area. Section 9 sets up the council in which each of those parties will be represented, in order to deal with matters relating to the application of the treaty. The council is organized in such a way as to be able to meet on short notice and at any time.
According to the next section, the signatories may invite to adhere to the treaty any other European state which is in a position to encourage the development of the principles of this treaty and to contribute to the security of the North Atlantic. This summarizes some of the provisions of the Atlantic charter. This document will become law in regard to the respect of borders; it is a treaty which might throw in the not too distant future a bright ray of hope on the road to peace and world security so earnestly wished for.
By the same token, consideration should be given to the drafting of a pact similar to the Atlantic pact for the nations of the Pacific. This mutual understanding, good will and harmony sought for the signatories of the Atlantic pact is also ardently desired for those of the Pacific. Free nations intend to establish peace and nothing will be neglected in order to attain that goal.
As someone said previously in this house, we detest communism in all its forms, whether it manifests itself in Europe or in Asia. We shall do our utmost in order to stamp it out wherever it may be, and in this connection, Mr. Speaker, I think that in view of the extraordinary sacrifices
already made by our citizens, no reproach could be addressed to a nation of barely fourteen million people. Obviously, violence has never settled any problem, and our military preparations are intended to checkmate the world domination ambitions of the communists.
Alas, when a regime refuses to acknowledge human rights, when it disregards indi-viduaj freedom and refuses to the citizen the right to worship and to adore the God of his choice, nothing good can come of it. The world today longs for a return of a sound prosperity, but it seems to seek in vain the proper formula in the maze in which it finds itself after two world wars and a depression which started barely twenty years tago.
I believe that a proper solution can only be found in a closer co-operation between peoples. What is lacking, no doubt, is a larger measure of charity. Suspicion is rife in both camps. 1 realize that the activities of Moscow are not very reassuring in regard to the maintenance of peace. We are witnessing an armaments race; nations are being placed on a war footing while ardently wishing to safeguard peace.
However, there still exists in the world a wise spiritual authority able to give us the necessary guidance to enable us to achieve understanding and harmony. This guiding light towards which most of the nations of the world are turning today for leadership possesses twenty centuries of experience, and a wealth of information which it would be greatly to our advantage to consult.
Let us hope that in the near future we shall have our own representative accredited to this authority in that city of the seven hills, thus enabling us to pursue a task so well begun.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already taken part in this debate on the motion to go into supply. I have not had an opportunity, however, to speak on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). Before doing so, I shall attempt, nevertheless, to reply briefly to the accusations levied the other night by the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon). I regret he is not here at the moment.
The hon. member said, amongst other things: Why are our troops not being brought back from Korea? It is essential, I feel, that we should go back to consider the reasons that prompted this parliament to approve the

sending of one brigade to Korea to be part of the United Nations troops that were to resist and repel aggression.
It will be remembered that in June, 1950, the North Koreans attacked South Korea, at a time when a United Nations commission was already out there trying to find a solution to the problem of unification of that country. The security council met at once and unanimously decided-owing to the absence of the soviet who have doubtlessly regretted their action ever since-to oppose force to this unjustified aggression in North Korea.
The security council appealed to the member governments of the United Nations, asking them to send land, sea and air forces to Korea, to take part in operations designed to resist that aggression.
Under the United Nations charter, Canada had undertaken to take part in any United Nations program for collective defence, at the request of the security council.
By sending a brigade to Korea, we have thus fulfilled a legal obligation to which we had freely subscribed, in order to sanction the principle of collective security; in our modern world, peace would be unattainable without that principle, for we are at all times exposed to the dangers of unjust aggression. At the outset, in the fall of 1950, fortune seemed to favour us and already, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has said,-and he was quoted the other evening by the hon. member for Chicoutimi,-we had high hopes of bringing peace back to Korea.
However, because of circumstances which it is not for me to judge, because a military leader saw fit to pursue a campaign which might have more wisely been stopped there and then, the Chinese thought they were in danger and entered the war. We believe that they were never faced with any real danger, but they claim that they had to defend their country. And in order to defend their country, they approved of the sending across the border of Chinese "volunteers" to help the North Koreans.
The United Nations forces had to withdraw and to reorganize in order to launch a new attack which brought them to the 38th parallel. At that moment, that is, last summer, armistice negotiations were started, while the opponents were facing each other along that 150-mile long front.
Since then, the front has remained about the same; there has been little activity, except for air fighting and some patrol clashes.
External Affairs
"What are we waiting for? Why do we not withdraw from Korea," asks the member for Chicoutimi?
If we keep in mind what I have just said, if we make a logical study of the facts such as I have recited them, how must we answer the member for Chicoutimi? Well, we are waiting until there has been an armistice or until this aggression has been really beaten back and the problem definitely settled. That it seems to me, is the motive by which Canadians must be guided, and the same motives should guide the other members of the United Nations with forces in Korea.
If the Americans, the British, the French, the Canadians, the Australians and the New Zealanders were to withdraw from Korea, what would happen? Immediately, North Korea and the Chinese communists would invade South Korea. What would the United Nations think then? What a let-down that would be for the world, for all those countries that have put their faith in that organization.
I said in this house, on Tuesday last, that we still believe and that we must keep on believing in the United Nations, for this organization can still establish and maintain world peace.
Let us hope that the Russians, at a certain moment, will see the light and will understand that it is in their own interest, as well as in their satellites' interest, to co-operate readily with the other member nations, because the United Nations offer a solid basis for peace, provided every one contributes to the undertaking and acts in good faith.
If Canadians were to set a bad example by withdrawing from Korea at this most crucial moment when this problem may well be in process of settlement, well, Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. member for Chicoutimi that, should we set such an example, no human being in this world would ever have faith in the United Nations and any other international body set up for joint defence would become useless.
We must not wait to be crushed by our potential enemies one after the other.
I happened to read the other day that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization was taking the spotlight away from the United Nations Organization and that NATO was threatening to throw into the background the aims and endeavours of the United Nations. I do not believe that is the case, Mr. Speaker. Our country and the other North Atlantic

External Affairs
treaty countries have had to rebuild and rearrange their defensive strength, in order to meet possible aggression, by establishing this Atlantic pact under section 51 of the United Nations charter, which allows member countries to unite for purposes of defence.
Well, if on the one hand, we were forced to do so, I repeat that on the other hand our long-term policy consists in uniting, within the United Nations Organization, for our common defence against a potential aggressor. We have given proof of this in Korea. It is true that at the present time, the work undertaken by NATO affects us more closely and costs us much more than our participation in the United Nations.
The North Atlantic pact is absolutely essential. Several hon. members have elaborated on that subject, among them the member for Prescott (Mr. Bruneau) who has just made a speech along those lines; the North Atlantic treaty must be considered as a means of avoiding aggression launched by potential enemies, as well as of reinforcing our strength and of helping the western countries to become stronger within the United Nations. I know not whether my chief, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will approve of what I have to say but personally I believe, and I shall keep on repeating it, that we can win peace only if we succeed in establishing a balance of power. World history itself backs up our assertion and proves that in spite of a few skirmishes, there has been peace in the world whenever a true balance of power has existed. Through the agency of NATO we can attain that equilibrium in the world and group under the United Nations equal forces having equal voices in any decision.
And it is not because we have to rearm within the framework of NATO that our actions are not consistent with the disarmament we preach at the United Nations. On the contrary, if we must defend ourselves against possible attack, if we have to rearm within the framework of NATO, this rearmament in itself is a means of bringing about the disarmament of the soviet bloc. That in my opinion is the only way to achieve that result since I believe the soviet bloc understands little else but force and that we will be in no position to negotiate on equal terms until our forces reach the point of balance of which I was speaking a moment ago.
It is unfortunate, obviously, that we have to require of the Canadian people their present sacrifices. It is not always easy to explain to some people that a country such as ours, occupying the northern part of the North American continent, may be concerned with what goes on in Europe and Asia. We have no other aim than the common security of the free nations.
For we must not imagine, Mr. Speaker, that we would spend less money, that taxes would be lower, if we allowed Russia to invade Europe or communist China to take over Asia. If we were to erect an impassable barrier around the American continent, behind which we would have to tighten our belts to a point that we could hardly breathe, I wonder what our standard of life would be, what taxes we would have to pay; I even wonder what we would have to eat. After all, that is the situation.
When we are called upon to meet our obligations in the international field it is our own interest we look after. We trust the Canadian people will realize that the sacrifices they are asked to bear are light compared to those that would be their lot should, unfortunately, the North American continent or the whole American continent come to fall under soviet control. There would then be no hope left. We would be living in jail on bread and water, and I am not sure, as I said, we would even be able to breathe.
